title: What technology is
description: Technology is knowledge put to work on the practical jobs of daily life, from stone tools to light switches.

facts.text: Britannica defines technology as the application of scientific knowledge to the practical aims of human life.
Stone tools from Lomekwi 3 in Kenya, about 3.3 million years old, are the oldest known and predate the genus Homo.
Our species, Homo sapiens, evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago.

title: Inventions that changed daily life
description: A few big inventions, from stone tools and the wheel to printing and the electric light, reshaped everyday life; nearly all of them are very recent.

facts.text: Wheels appear in Mesopotamia by about 3500 BCE, both on carts (a Sumerian pictograph of a wheeled sledge) and as the potter's wheel.
Johannes Gutenberg built Europe's first known mechanized printing press and printed his Bible around 1455, making books far cheaper to produce.
In 1879 Thomas Edison developed a carbon-filament incandescent light bulb.

Squeezing 3.3 million years of tools into 24 hours, Homo sapiens (300,000 years) arrives at about 9:49 p.m., wheels (about 3500 BCE) about 2.5 minutes before midnight, Volta's 1800 battery about 6 seconds before, and Edison's 1879 bulb under 4 seconds before.

title: What energy is
description: Energy is the ability to do work. It is stored (potential) or working (kinetic) and is measured in joules.

facts.text: Scientists define energy as the ability (capacity) to do work.

Energy is potential (stored), such as chemical energy in food and batteries, gravitational energy in raised objects and energy in stretched rubber bands, or kinetic (working): motion, heat, light, sound and electricity.
The joule is the SI unit of energy: the work done by a force of one newton acting over one meter.
One joule is about the energy needed to lift a small apple (about 100 grams) one meter.

title: Energy changes form
description: Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another; in most conversions a lot of it ends up as heat.

facts.text: Energy is neither created nor destroyed; when it is used it changes from one form into another.
Food contains chemical energy, which your body stores and turns into kinetic energy when you move.
At best the human body turns only about a quarter of its food energy into motion; most becomes heat, and most of the time the useful share is far lower.

title: Electric current
description: Current is moving charge, counted in amperes. Electrons already in the wire drift slowly, but the push travels almost at light speed.

facts.text: Electrons carry negative charge and protons positive charge; opposite charges attract and like charges repel.
An electric current is a movement of electric charge; in metal wires the moving charges are electrons.
The charge carriers in a wire are electrons belonging to the wire's own atoms; a battery supplies energy, not charge, and charge is not used up in a circuit.
Electrons in a typical wire drift very slowly, roughly a meter or two per hour (about 10^-4 meters per second).
Closing a switch sends the electrical push through the circuit at nearly the speed of light, so electrons everywhere start moving at once.
One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge per second, about 6.2 billion billion (6.2 x 10^18) electrons per second.

title: Voltage
description: Voltage is the energy given to each coulomb of charge: one volt is one joule per coulomb.

facts.text: Voltage measures the energy given to each unit of charge: one volt is one joule per coulomb (NIST: V = W/A, W = J/s, C = A s).
A common teaching analogy compares a battery to the pump that lifts water to the top of a water-park slide: it gives charge energy to flow around the circuit.
Common household battery cells, such as AA cells, provide about 1.5 volts each.

title: Circuits and switches
description: Current flows only around a closed loop of conductors; a switch opens or closes a gap in that loop.

facts.text: An electric circuit is a path for current made of an energy source (such as a battery), devices that use the current (such as lamps) and connecting wires.
Current flows only around a closed conducting loop from one terminal of the source to the other; a break anywhere in a single loop stops the current everywhere in it.
A switch in the open ("off") position leaves a gap, so there is no closed loop and no current; closing it completes the loop.
Metals such as copper are conductors that carry charge easily; materials like paper and plastic are insulators that stop the flow.

title: Series and parallel circuits
description: In series, devices share one path and fail together; homes are wired in parallel so each device has its own branch.

facts.text: In a series circuit everything is on one path: if one bulb is removed the others go out, and a kitchen wired in series would need every appliance on for the fridge to run.
Home wiring is parallel: each light or appliance is on its own branch with the same voltage across it and draws the current it needs.

title: The incandescent bulb
description: An incandescent bulb makes light by heating a tungsten filament until it glows, wasting most of its energy as heat.

facts.text: Incandescent bulbs waste about 90% of their energy as heat; only about 10% becomes light.
In an incandescent bulb, current heats a thin filament that resists it until the filament is hot enough to glow.
Modern filaments are tungsten, which has the highest melting point of the suitable materials.
The glass bulb holds a vacuum or an inert gas so the filament does not oxidize (burn away).
Scientists around the world worked on the incandescent lamp for about 40 years before Edison, and Joseph Swan in England made a similar carbon-filament lamp in 1878.
Edison's team kept testing filaments and settled on bamboo, giving lamps a lifetime of up to 1,200 hours.

title: The LED
description: An LED makes light directly from a semiconductor junction, with no hot filament, using far less energy.

facts.text: An LED (light-emitting diode) is a semiconductor device with no filament: when current crosses the junction between two semiconductor materials, electrons release energy as light, and the material sets the color.
LEDs use at least 75% less energy than incandescent bulbs and last many times longer.

title: Volta's first battery
description: Galvani's twitching frog legs led Volta to build the voltaic pile in 1800, the first reliable battery.

facts.text: In 1791 Luigi Galvani saw frog leg muscles twitch when touched with two different metals and called it "animal electricity"; Volta argued the current came from the metals and the frog only conducted it.

In 1800 Volta built the voltaic pile, alternating zinc and silver (or copper) discs separated by cloth or paper soaked in salt water: the first reliable battery, giving a continuous current, which vindicated his view against Galvani's.
The volt, the unit of voltage, was named in Volta's honor in 1881.

title: How a battery works
description: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy, sending electrons from anode to cathode through the outside circuit; it dies when its reactants are used up.

facts.text: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy: electrons leave the anode, travel through the outside circuit to the cathode, and ions move through the electrolyte inside to balance them.

A battery stops working when its reacting chemicals are used up; a rechargeable one is restored by driving current through it in reverse, which runs the reaction backward and stores chemical energy again.

title: Electricity makes magnetism
description: An electric current makes a magnetic field, as Ørsted saw in 1820; a coil of wire becomes a switchable electromagnet.

facts.text: During an evening lecture in April 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted saw a magnetic compass needle swing to line up across a current-carrying wire: evidence that electricity and magnetism are linked.
Every magnet has a north and a south pole; opposite poles attract and like poles repel.
An electric current makes a magnetic field; current loops are the most common source of magnetic fields.
An electromagnet is a coil of wire around a magnetic core such as iron; its magnetism can be switched on and off, strengthened or reversed by changing the current.

title: The electric motor
description: A motor spins a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field, reversing the current each half turn to keep it going; Faraday built the first in 1821.

facts.text: In a motor, a current-carrying coil between magnetic poles feels a turning force that spins a shaft; brushes and a commutator reverse the coil's current every half turn so it keeps turning the same way.
An electric motor turns electrical energy into mechanical energy (motion).
Electric motors run household devices such as fans, pumps, drills, hair dryers and electric toothbrushes.
In 1821 Michael Faraday built the first electric motor, making a current-carrying wire circle around a magnet in a bath of mercury.

title: Electromagnetic induction
description: A changing magnetic field through a coil induces a current, as Faraday found in 1831.

facts.text: In 1831 Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet inside a coil of wire makes (induces) an electric current in the wire.
Induction needs a changing magnetic field: a steady field through a coil induces nothing, and the faster the field changes, the larger the voltage.

title: The generator
description: A generator is a motor run in reverse: turbines spin a rotor inside coils to turn motion into electricity.

facts.text: A generator is a motor run in reverse: force the coil to turn in the magnetic field and current comes out; the same device can work as either.
A generator converts mechanical energy (motion) into electrical energy.
A power-station generator has fixed wire coils (the stator) around a spinning electromagnet (the rotor); turning the rotor makes current flow in the coils.
Generators are spun by turbines driven by steam, falling water, wind or burning gas; most US and world electricity comes from turbine-driven generators.
Solar photovoltaic cells are the exception: they turn sunlight directly into electricity, with no spinning generator.

title: AC and DC
description: Direct current flows one way; alternating current keeps reversing, 60 cycles a second on the US grid, one cycle per turn of a two-pole generator.

facts.text: Direct current (DC) flows steadily in one direction, as from a battery; alternating current (AC) keeps reversing direction.
US grid AC runs at 60 hertz, 60 complete back-and-forth cycles per second; most grids use 50 or 60.
A two-pole generator must spin at 3,600 revolutions per minute (60 turns a second) to make 60-hertz AC, one cycle per turn.
The grid still runs mainly on AC, but LEDs, computers, solar cells and electric vehicles run on DC.

title: Why AC won
description: AC beat Edison's DC because transformers can raise its voltage for efficient long-distance transmission and lower it for homes.

facts.text: On September 4, 1882, Edison's Pearl Street station in New York began supplying direct current to a district of one-quarter square mile: the forerunner of all central power stations.
Transformers change voltage by induction, so they need a changing current: they work with AC but not with steady DC.
DC could not easily be converted to higher or lower voltages, which made sending it long distances a problem; AC could, using transformers.
Higher voltage makes long-distance transmission more efficient and cheaper, while lower voltage is safer in homes; transformers step between them.
From the late 1880s Edison and Tesla fought the War of the Currents; Edison claimed AC was more dangerous and publicly electrocuted animals to prove it.
Westinghouse won the bid to light the 1893 Chicago World's Fair with Tesla's AC, and on November 16, 1896, Buffalo was lit with AC from Niagara Falls.

title: Watts and kilowatt-hours
description: Power is how fast energy flows: a watt is a joule per second, volts times amps; bills charge for energy in kilowatt-hours.

facts.text: One watt is one joule per second, so a 60-watt bulb uses 60 joules of energy every second it is on.
Volts times amperes gives watts: joules per coulomb times coulombs per second equals joules per second.
A kilowatt-hour is 1,000 watts for one hour (3,600 seconds): 3.6 million joules.
Utilities measure electricity in kilowatt-hours, and household electricity is priced per kilowatt-hour.

title: How power reaches your socket
description: Electricity is stepped up to high voltage for long transmission lines, then stepped down at substations and near homes; the lower 48 US states run on three main grids.

facts.text: The power grid of the lower 48 US states is made up of three main interconnections that mostly operate independently: the Eastern, the Western, and ERCOT, which covers most of Texas.

Electricity from a power plant is stepped up by a transformer, carried long distances on high-voltage transmission lines, stepped down at substations, and delivered on lower-voltage distribution lines through a final transformer near the customer.
US transmission lines typically run at 230 kV to 765 kV (230,000 to 765,000 volts).
For safety, voltage is reduced to 120, 240 or 480 volts at the user's site; US homes get 120 and 240 volts.
765,000 volts is more than 6,000 times the 120 volts of a home circuit (765,000 / 120 = 6,375).
Power is sent long distances at high voltage because less current is needed for the same power, which means less energy lost in the lines.

title: Balancing the grid
description: Grid operators must match electricity supply to demand at every moment, or blackouts can happen.

facts.text: Grid operators must call on power plants to supply the right amount of electricity at every moment; balancing authorities keep supply and demand precisely balanced, and if they fall out of balance, local or widespread blackouts can happen.

title: Steam power plants
description: Coal and many gas plants burn fuel to boil water; the steam spins a turbine and generator, and most of the fuel's energy is lost as heat.

facts.text: Steam turbines generate most of the world's electricity; they are heated by fossil fuels, nuclear fission, biomass, geothermal or solar thermal energy.
In a steam power plant, fuel burned in a boiler heats water into steam; the steam pushes on blades attached to a shaft, spinning the turbine, which drives a generator.

In 2024 the average US coal plant used about 10,777 Btu of fuel per kilowatt-hour, turning only about a third (about 32%) of the fuel's energy into electricity; about two-thirds ended up as waste heat.
In 2025, natural gas was the top source of US utility-scale electricity at about 41%, coal made about 17%, and fossil fuels together about 58%; petroleum made only about 0.7%.

title: Gas turbines and combined cycle
description: Gas turbines spin directly on hot gases; combined-cycle plants reuse the exhaust heat to make steam for a second turbine, getting more electricity from the same fuel.

facts.text: A combustion gas turbine, similar to a jet engine, burns fuel to make hot gases that spin its blades directly; a combined-cycle plant uses the hot exhaust from a gas turbine to make steam for a steam turbine, getting more electricity from the same fuel.
In 2024 the average US natural gas plant used about 7,754 Btu per kilowatt-hour, turning about 44% of its fuel's energy into electricity, compared with about 32% for coal.

title: How oil forms and is found
description: Crude oil formed from ancient marine life under heat and pressure, sits in tiny spaces in rock, and is reached by drilling wells.

facts.text: Crude oil is found in underground reservoirs, in tiny spaces within sedimentary rocks, not in open underground lakes.

Crude oil formed from the remains of tiny marine plants and animals (such as diatoms) that lived millions of years ago; buried under layers of sand, silt and rock, they were turned into oil by heat and pressure.
Petroleum, natural gas and coal store chemical energy in the bonds of their molecules.

On August 27, 1859, Edwin Drake's well near Titusville, Pennsylvania, struck oil at a depth of 69 feet (21 meters): the first productive oil well in the United States, which launched the modern petroleum industry.
To reach oil, wells are drilled down through layers of sand, silt and rock to the rock formations that hold oil and gas.

title: Refining and using oil
description: Refineries separate crude by boiling point and crack heavy molecules into fuels like gasoline; oil mostly powers transport, not the grid.

facts.text: Refining begins with distillation: heated crude oil separates by boiling point in a distillation tower, with the lightest parts rising as vapor to the top and the heaviest settling at the bottom.
Cracking uses heat, pressure, catalysts and sometimes hydrogen to break heavy hydrocarbon molecules into lighter ones, such as those in gasoline.
From a 42-gallon barrel of crude oil, US refineries make on average about 19 to 20 gallons of gasoline, 11 to 13 gallons of distillate (mostly diesel) and 3 to 5 gallons of jet fuel.
In 2025, petroleum products supplied about 89% of the energy used for US transportation.

title: How nuclear power works
description: Neutrons split uranium-235 atoms in a controlled chain reaction; the heat makes steam to spin a turbine, with no CO2 released while running.

facts.text: According to the US Department of Energy, one uranium fuel pellet produces as much energy as about one ton of coal.
Nuclear plants use uranium-235, whose atoms split easily; the uranium is made into small ceramic pellets stacked in sealed metal tubes called fuel rods.
In fission, a neutron strikes a uranium atom and splits it, releasing a large amount of energy as heat and radiation, plus more neutrons.
Neutrons released by one split go on to split other uranium atoms, a chain reaction; reactors control it, inserting control rods to slow it and withdrawing them to speed it up.
In a nuclear plant, heat from fission turns water into steam, which spins a turbine to produce electricity.
Nuclear reactors do not produce air pollution or carbon dioxide while operating.
Nuclear power made about 18% of US utility-scale electricity in 2025 and about 9% of the world's electricity.

title: The nuclear debate
description: Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years; groups such as the IEA and Greenpeace weigh nuclear power's role very differently.

facts.text: Spent nuclear fuel is highly radioactive and can remain dangerous for thousands of years; the US has no permanent disposal facility, so it is stored in pools of water and dry containers.

The IEA says nuclear power can play a major role in secure transitions to low-emissions energy; Greenpeace opposes new nuclear plants, calling nuclear power dangerous and expensive and citing waste and the Chernobyl and Fukushima accidents.

title: How a dam makes electricity
description: Water falling from a reservoir through a penstock turns a turbine and generator, turning gravitational energy into electricity.

facts.text: The first US hydroelectric plant to sell electricity opened on the Fox River in Appleton, Wisconsin, on September 30, 1882.
Appleton's hydro plant opened 26 days after Edison's Pearl Street station (September 4 to September 30, 1882).
Thousands of years ago, people used hydropower to turn paddle wheels on rivers to grind grain.
At a hydroelectric dam, water stored in the reservoir enters an intake near the bottom of the dam, falls through a pipe called a penstock, and turns a turbine whose shaft drives a generator.

title: Head and flow
description: A hydro plant's output depends on how much water flows and how far it falls; hydropower is a much bigger share of the world's electricity than of US electricity.

facts.text: The amount of energy in moving water depends on the volume of the flow and the height it falls, called the head; the greater the flow and the higher the head, the more electricity a plant can make.
The Three Gorges Dam on China's Yangtze River is the world's biggest hydroelectric facility.
Hydropower made about 14% of the world's electricity in 2025 but only about 6% of US utility-scale electricity.

title: How a wind turbine works
description: Wind turns wing-shaped blades and a rotor that drives a generator in the nacelle atop a tall tower.

facts.text: A wind turbine's blades work like an airplane wing; the wind turns them and the rotor, which drives a generator directly or through a shaft and gearbox, housed in a nacelle on top of a tall tower.

title: Where wind works best
description: Wind power rises with the cube of wind speed, so turbines go on windy plains, hilltops, water and tall towers.

facts.text: The power in the wind is proportional to the cube of the wind speed, so doubling the wind speed gives eight times the power (2 x 2 x 2 = 8).
Good sites for utility-scale wind turbines have average wind speeds of at least 13 mph (5.8 m/s), such as smooth rounded hilltops, open plains and water, and mountain gaps that funnel wind.
Wind speeds are generally higher farther above the ground, which is why turbines stand on tall towers.
In 2025, Texas, Iowa, Oklahoma, Kansas and Illinois produced about 52% of US wind electricity, and wind made about a tenth (about 10% to 11%) of US utility-scale electricity.

title: How solar cells work
description: Sunlight knocks electrons loose in a semiconductor cell, making current with nothing spinning; panels have grown far more efficient since 1954.

facts.text: In 2025, solar PV overtook wind as a source of world electricity for the first time, according to the International Energy Agency.

A PV cell is made of a semiconductor; when it absorbs enough sunlight, electrons are knocked loose and move toward the front surface, creating a charge imbalance like a battery's two terminals, and connecting the cell into a circuit lets current flow.
The first practical photovoltaic cell was developed in 1954 by Bell Telephone researchers.
The efficiency of commercial PV panels (the share of sunlight they turn into electricity) averaged under 10% in the mid-1980s, about 15% by 2015, and is approaching 25% for state-of-the-art modules.
PV systems can charge batteries to provide electricity when the sun is not shining.

title: Solar DC and inverters
description: Solar cells make direct current, so inverters convert it to the grid's alternating current.

facts.text: PV cells make direct current (DC); inverters convert it to alternating current (AC).
PV cells are connected in weather-tight panels, and panels are grouped into arrays.

title: Why storing electricity is hard
description: Storage must convert electricity to another form and back, losing some on the way; big batteries now shift midday solar to the evening.

facts.text: US utility-scale battery capacity grew from about 8.8 gigawatts (about 9 billion watts) at the end of 2022 to 43.6 gigawatts (about 44 billion watts) at the end of 2025, about five times as much.
Energy storage systems make no electricity of their own: they must be charged with electricity from generators or the grid, and they use more electricity for charging than they give back.
Grid storage systems in use keep energy in other forms: water pumped uphill, batteries (electrochemical), heat, compressed air and flywheels.
In California, batteries charged with extra midday solar supplied an average of 4.9 GW during the 5 to 9 p.m. evening peak in 2025, up from under 1 GW in 2022, displacing natural gas generation.

title: Pumped-storage hydropower
description: Pumped storage pumps water uphill with spare electricity and lets it run back through turbines when power is needed.

facts.text: Pumped-storage hydropower uses grid electricity to run turbines in reverse, pumping water up to a storage reservoir; when needed, the water flows back down through the turbines to generate electricity.
Rocky River in Connecticut, the oldest US pumped-storage plant, began pumping water in 1928.

title: How CO2 warms the planet
description: CO2 traps heat; burning coal, oil and gas has raised it more than 50%, and the IPCC finds humans have unequivocally warmed the planet.

facts.text: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide trap heat from sunlight, warming the planet.
Carbon dioxide in the air has risen by more than 50% since industrial times began in the 18th century, mainly from burning coal, oil and gas.

The IPCC, the UN body that assesses climate science, finds that human activities, principally greenhouse gas emissions, have unequivocally caused global warming, with global surface temperature about 1.1°C above 1850–1900 in 2011–2020.

title: Emissions by power source
description: Coal emits the most CO2 per kilowatt-hour, gas about half as much, and wind, solar, nuclear and hydro far less over their whole lives.

facts.text: In 2023, US coal-fired electricity released about 2.3 pounds (2.31) of CO2 per kilowatt-hour and natural gas about 0.96 pounds, less than half as much.

Over a plant's whole life, the IPCC's 2014 review found median emissions of about 820 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for coal, 490 for gas combined cycle, 48 for utility solar, 24 for hydropower, 12 for nuclear and 11 for onshore wind.
Coal's median lifecycle emissions (820 grams per kWh) are more than 70 times onshore wind's (11 grams); 820 / 11 is about 75.
Wind, solar and nuclear power have zero direct emissions; their lifecycle emissions come mostly from building the plants and their supply chains.

title: Debating the energy path
description: Countries set the Paris goal; named groups such as OPEC and Greenpeace disagree sharply on how fast to move away from fossil fuels.

facts.text: In the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries agreed to aim to hold global warming well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

OPEC projects that oil demand will keep growing to almost 123 million barrels a day by 2050 and stresses the need for continued investment in oil; Greenpeace calls for a fast and fair phase-out of coal, oil and gas.

title: The world's electricity mix
description: In 2025 coal and renewables each made about a third of the world's electricity, gas about a fifth, and low-emissions sources more than 40%.

facts.text: In 2025, coal made about 34% (about a third) of the world's electricity, renewables together about a third, and natural gas about a fifth.
Low-emissions sources, renewables plus nuclear, made more than 40% of the world's electricity in 2025, according to the IEA.

title: Simple machines
description: Levers, wheels and axles and pulleys are simple machines: a lever multiplies a push by the ratio of its arm lengths, a wheel and axle by the ratio of its radii.

facts.text: Plutarch reported that Archimedes (3rd century BCE) moved a loaded ship on land with a system of compound pulleys; the story cannot be checked.
The six classical simple machines are the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge and screw.
A lever turns on a pivot (fulcrum); force times distance from the fulcrum balances on each side, so an effort five times farther out than the load is multiplied five times.
In a wheel and axle, force applied at the large wheel is multiplied at the axle by the ratio of their radii.

title: Trading force for distance
description: A pulley system shares a load among its rope strands, cutting the force needed, but you pull proportionally more rope: no machine puts out more work than goes in.

facts.text: The mechanical advantage of a pulley system is about the number of rope strands supporting the load: with 4 strands, you pull with about a quarter of the force.
A machine cannot do more work than the energy put into it: with 4 supporting strands you pull 4 meters of rope to lift a load 1 meter, and friction takes a little extra.

title: Newcomen's steam engine
description: Newcomen's 1712 engine pumped water from mines: it condensed steam under a piston to make a partial vacuum, and air pressure pushed the piston down.

facts.text: The first recorded Newcomen engine was built near Dudley Castle, England, in 1712; such engines pumped water out of mines, a job horses did at high cost.
A steam engine uses steam to do mechanical work through heat: hot steam, usually made in a separate boiler, pushes a piston in a cylinder.
In Newcomen's engine, a spray of cold water condensed the steam in the cylinder, leaving a partial vacuum, and atmospheric pressure pushed the piston down.

title: Watt's steam engine
description: James Watt's separate condenser (1765, patented 1769) kept the cylinder hot and cut fuel costs; from 1781 his engines turned a shaft, and the watt is named for him.

facts.text: James Watt conceived the separate condenser in 1765 and patented it in 1769; condensing steam outside the cylinder avoided heating and cooling it each stroke and cut fuel costs.
In 1781 Watt's sun-and-planet gear let his engine turn a shaft, so it could drive factory machines as well as pumps.
The watt, the SI unit of power (one joule per second), is named for James Watt to honor his work on engine efficiency.

title: Factories and the Industrial Revolution
description: The Industrial Revolution moved work from homes into powered factories with divided labor; steam freed mills from riversides so they could grow in towns.

facts.text: The first Industrial Revolution, mostly in Britain from the mid-18th century to about 1830, changed an agrarian, handicraft economy into one dominated by industry and machine manufacturing.
Machines such as the spinning jenny and the power loom increased production with less human effort.
Before Arkwright's mills most cotton spinning was done at home; he moved it into huge powered mills with hundreds of workers.
In 1771 Arkwright began building a water-powered cotton-spinning mill at Cromford, beside the fast-flowing River Derwent.
The factory system brought increased division of labor: each worker specialized in part of the job.
Water power tied mills to suitable rivers; steam engines let mill owners build near existing pools of workers, and cities grew.
Arkwright's Miller Street mill in Manchester was the first spinning mill to make use of steam power.

title: Factory work and the first factory laws
description: Factory work meant long, clock-driven shifts, often for children; Britain's 1833 Factory Act banned under-9s from textile mills and sent inspectors to enforce it.

facts.text: In the earliest days of Arkwright's mills, production went on around the clock, with two 13-hour shifts a day.
Industrial workers faced long hours of tedious and often dangerous work at subsistence wages, and children worked in the mills too.
Britain's Factory Act of 1833 banned children under 9 from textile mills, limited ages 9 to 12 to 8 hours a day, and created inspectors: the first such act with enforcement.

title: The internal combustion engine
description: A car engine burns fuel inside its cylinders, where a spark ignites fuel and air; only about 12%-30% of the fuel energy moves the car, and most of the rest is lost as heat.

facts.text: Only about 12%-30% of the energy in the fuel put in a conventional car moves it down the road; most of the rest is lost in the engine, mainly as heat.
In a gasoline internal combustion engine, fuel mixed with air is ignited by a spark plug inside the combustion chamber, and the hot expanding gases push the piston.

title: The four-stroke cycle
description: Intake, compression, power and exhaust: only the power stroke pushes, and a crankshaft turns the piston's up-and-down motion into rotation.

facts.text: The four strokes are intake (fuel and air drawn in), compression (the mix squeezed), power (a spark ignites it and expanding gas pushes the piston) and exhaust (burned gases pushed out).
A connecting rod turns the piston's back-and-forth motion into the crankshaft's rotation; each four-stroke cycle takes two crankshaft revolutions.
Nikolaus Otto built an engine on the four-stroke principle in 1876; the French engineer Alphonse Beau de Rochas had patented the cycle earlier.

title: How an electric car works
description: An all-electric car drives its wheels with an electric motor powered by a battery pack; counting from the plug, over 77% of the energy reaches the wheels.

facts.text: By 1900, electric cars accounted for around a third of all vehicles on the road; cheap gasoline cars such as the Model T and the electric starter then pushed them aside.
In 2025, global electric car sales (battery electric plus plug-in hybrids) exceeded 20 million, about 1 in 4 new cars sold (IEA, Global EV Outlook 2026).
An all-electric car has an electric traction motor powered by a rechargeable battery pack instead of an internal combustion engine, and no tailpipe exhaust.
Counting from the grid, electric cars convert over 77% of the electrical energy to power at the wheels; gasoline cars convert about 12%-30% of their fuel energy.

title: Regenerative braking
description: When an electric car slows, the turning wheels drive its motor as a generator, recharging the battery instead of wasting all the energy of motion.

facts.text: Regenerative braking uses the wheels' forward motion to turn the motor, which generates electricity for the battery and helps slow the vehicle, recapturing energy normally lost in braking.

title: Friction
description: Friction resists surfaces sliding over each other; rough surfaces catch, starting to slide takes more force than keeping going, and friction lets you grip the ground.

facts.text: Friction is a force that resists one surface sliding over another; even smooth-looking surfaces are rough up close, and their bumps catch.
Starting an object sliding takes more force than keeping it sliding: static friction is greater than kinetic friction.
Friction provides the traction you need to walk without slipping.

title: How brakes stop a car
description: Friction brakes press pads on a spinning disc and turn the energy of motion into heat; energy of motion grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples braking distance.

facts.text: When surfaces rub, friction turns energy of motion into heat, which is why rubbing your hands warms them.
A disc brake presses friction pads against a metal disc that turns with the wheel, turning the vehicle's energy of motion into heat.
A car at 100 km/h has four times the energy of motion it has at 50 km/h, so with the same braking force, doubling speed quadruples braking distance.

title: Gear ratios
description: Meshing gears cannot slip, so their tooth counts set the speed ratio: a driven gear with twice the teeth turns at half the speed.

facts.text: Gears pass rotation through meshing teeth without slipping; a driven gear with twice as many teeth as the gear driving it turns at half the speed, with twice the torque.

The Antikythera mechanism, recovered in 1901 from an ancient Greek shipwreck and made around 100 BCE, over 2,000 years ago, has 30 surviving bronze gears whose gear trains modeled astronomical cycles and predicted eclipses.

title: Gears trade speed for force
description: A small gear driving a big one gives more turning force at lower speed; a big gear driving a small one gives speed instead, like a bike's low and high gears.

facts.text: A bicycle's low gear (small front chainring, large rear sprocket) makes pedaling easier but slower, which helps on steep climbs.
When a larger gear drives a smaller one, the pair increases speed and reduces turning force (torque).
Gears, like a wheel and axle, have a mechanical advantage set by the ratio of their radii.

title: Pascal's principle
description: Press on a liquid at rest in a closed container and the pressure rises equally everywhere in it; liquids barely compress, so they pass a push along.

facts.text: Pascal's principle, described by Blaise Pascal: a pressure change applied to a fluid at rest in a closed container is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the walls.
Liquids are nearly incompressible: they can hardly be squeezed into a smaller volume.
Through a hydraulic system, a relatively small force can be magnified enough to lift a car.

title: Hydraulic force multiplication
description: Equal pressure on a piston with 10 times the area gives 10 times the force, but the small piston moves 10 times as far; car brakes work this way.

facts.text: In a hydraulic system the pressure is the same on both pistons, so a piston with 10 times the area pushes with 10 times the force (F1/A1 = F2/A2).
Hydraulics multiply force but not work: the small piston moves proportionally farther, 10 times as far for 10 times the force, so to raise the big one 1 centimeter it travels 10.
Car brakes are hydraulic: the driver's push on the pedal is carried by brake fluid to pistons at the wheels, giving larger braking forces, with the same pressure acting on every brake.

title: Balancing a bike by steering
description: A rider stays up by steering the wheels back under the falling bike, the way a hand moves under a balanced broom; a stopped bike cannot do this.

facts.text: In 1817 Karl von Drais rode his wooden two-wheeler, with handlebar steering and no pedals, 14 km, pushing it along with his feet on the ground.
Riders balance by steering to bring the wheels, the base of support, back under the center of mass, much like the hand motions that balance a broomstick.

title: Why some bikes balance themselves
description: A moving riderless bike can steer itself into a lean and recover; in 2011 a bike with neither gyroscopic effect nor trail still did, so the full reason is a subtle mix of effects.

facts.text: A riderless bicycle moving fast enough steers itself into a lean and recovers from a sideways push; the 2011 test bike did this above about 5 mph (8 km/h).
The common explanation for self-steering credited gyroscopic effects of the spinning front wheel or trail, the front contact point trailing behind the steering axis like a caster.
In 2011 Kooijman and colleagues (Science) built a bike with counter-rotating wheels to cancel the gyroscopic effect and negative trail; it still balanced itself, so neither is required.
Self-balance comes from a mix of effects linked to how mass is distributed, including the front assembly; researchers say much is still to be learned about bike balance.

title: Horsepower
description: James Watt set one horsepower at 33,000 foot-pounds per minute, about 746 watts, more than an average horse can keep up over a working day.

facts.text: James Watt adopted the horsepower in the late 18th century after experiments with strong dray horses; it is about 50% more than an average horse can sustain over a working day.
One horsepower is 33,000 foot-pounds of work per minute, about 746 watts, so 100 horsepower is about 74,600 watts (about 75 kilowatts).

title: The four forces of flight
description: Weight, lift, drag and thrust act on every plane; in steady flight lift balances weight and thrust balances drag.

facts.text: Four forces act on a plane in flight: weight pulls it toward Earth's center, lift opposes weight, drag resists its motion, and engine thrust overcomes drag.
In steady cruising flight lift equals weight and thrust equals drag; when the forces are unbalanced, the plane accelerates toward the largest force.

title: How a wing makes lift
description: A wing turns the passing air downward, so the air pushes it up; seen as pressure, faster air above the wing means lower pressure there. The equal-transit story is a myth.

facts.text: Lift occurs when a solid object turns a moving flow of air: the flow is turned one way and lift acts the opposite way, by Newton's third law.
A wing is shaped and tilted so air over it moves faster than air under it; faster air has lower pressure, so the wing is pushed up.
NASA says the pressure (Bernoulli) and flow-turning (Newton) explanations of lift are both correct descriptions of the same force.
NASA calls the equal transit theory incorrect: air over a wing's top does not meet the air below at the trailing edge; it arrives first.
Symmetric wings, flat paper airplanes and planes flying upside down, longer curved side at the bottom, all make lift, which equal transit cannot explain.
A wing's angle to the oncoming air, its angle of attack, has a large effect on lift; raising the nose at takeoff adds lift, but too steep a wing stalls.

title: Action and reaction push vehicles
description: Every engine that moves a vehicle accelerates a working fluid backward, and the reaction pushes the vehicle forward: Newton's third law.

facts.text: All thrust comes from Newton's third law, for every action an equal and opposite reaction: an engine accelerates a working fluid and the reaction pushes the vehicle.
A jet engine's working fluid is the surrounding air, and it makes thrust because the gas leaves the nozzle faster than the air came in.

title: The jet engine
description: A jet engine squeezes air in a compressor, burns fuel in it, spins a turbine that drives the compressor, and blasts the gas out of a nozzle. Airliners use turbofans.

facts.text: Frank Whittle obtained his first turbojet patent in Britain in 1930; an aircraft powered by his engine first flew on May 15, 1941.
Hans von Ohain designed a turbojet independently in Germany; it powered the He 178, the first jet aircraft to fly, on August 27, 1939.
In a jet engine, a compressor raises the air's pressure, fuel burns in the burner, the hot gas spins a turbine whose shaft drives the compressor, and a nozzle speeds the gas out.
In a turbofan, some air goes through the core and the rest bypasses it, like air through a propeller, adding thrust for nearly the same fuel; most modern airliners use them.
A jet (turbine) engine takes its oxygen from the surrounding air, so it cannot work in space, where there is no air.

title: Electric trains
description: Most modern trains are driven by electric motors: electric trains take current from an overhead wire or third rail, and diesel-electrics make it on board.

facts.text: Japan's Tokaido Shinkansen opened between Tokyo and Osaka in 1964; its electric trains, powered from an overhead wire, originally reached 210 km/h.
An electric locomotive picks up current from an overhead wire or a third rail and uses traction motors: it converts power rather than generating it.
Most diesel locomotives transmit power electrically: the diesel engine drives a generator whose current runs electric traction motors.

title: Maglev trains
description: A maglev train is lifted by magnets so no wheels touch its guideway, and guideway coils that keep changing polarity pull it along.

facts.text: In a maglev, magnets lift the train about 1.3 cm above its guideway with no wheels touching, and guideway coils that keep changing polarity propel it.
Shanghai's maglev began daily commercial service in January 2004, running at up to 430 km/h: the first high-speed maglev in commercial service.

title: Archimedes' principle
description: Water pushes up on a ship with a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside; a ship settles until that water weighs as much as the ship.

facts.text: Archimedes' principle: anything in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
A ship sinks into the water until the water it displaces weighs as much as the ship; loaded with cargo, it sinks deeper and displaces more.
Average density decides floating: a lump of clay sinks, but shaped into a boat it floats, and the same is true of steel ships, whose hulls enclose air.
Steel's density is about 7.8 grams per cubic centimeter, about 7.8 times that of water (1 gram per cubic centimeter).

title: The Plimsoll line
description: A mark on a ship's hull shows the deepest it may safely sit; separate marks allow for fresh water, which is less dense than seawater.

facts.text: After Samuel Plimsoll's campaign against overloaded ships, Britain's 1876 Merchant Shipping Act fixed a loading mark on hulls: the Plimsoll line.
The Plimsoll line marks the maximum depth a loaded ship may safely sit; if the ship is overloaded, the mark goes under water.
Fresh water is less dense than seawater, so the same ship sits deeper in fresh water; hulls carry separate fresh-water load marks.

title: Radar
description: Radar sends out radio pulses and times their echoes; half the round trip at the speed of light gives the distance, and the Doppler shift gives speed.

facts.text: In February 1935, Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins detected a bomber about 8 miles away from radio waves of the BBC's Daventry transmitter bouncing off it.
Radar (radio detection and ranging) sends radio pulses and finds distance from the round-trip time of the echo, out to the target and back.
Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 km per second, so a radar echo from 150 km away returns in about a thousandth of a second.
Radar reads the Doppler shift in an echo's frequency as a target's speed and direction; it is used for air traffic control, weather and speed enforcement.

title: Sonar
description: Sonar times echoes of sound pulses in water, where sound travels far and fast, to find the seafloor or objects.

facts.text: Sonar (sound navigation and ranging) sends a pulse of sound into water and times its echo; sound travels farther in water than radar or light waves.
Sound travels through seawater at about 1,500 meters per second, so an echo after 2 seconds has gone 3,000 meters round trip: a 1,500-meter depth.

title: How rockets work in space
description: A rocket pushes on its own exhaust, not on air, and carries its own oxidizer, so it works in a vacuum where jet engines cannot.

facts.text: A rocket burns propellant and its nozzle accelerates the hot exhaust out; the reaction to that exhaust, by Newton's third law, is the rocket's thrust.
A rocket carries its oxidizer on board with its fuel, so it can make thrust in a vacuum; in a liquid rocket both are pumped into a chamber and burned.

title: Goddard's rockets
description: Robert Goddard flew the first liquid-fueled rocket in 1926, after a 1920 newspaper editorial claimed rockets could not work in a vacuum.

facts.text: In 1920 The New York Times mocked Robert Goddard, saying rockets could not work in a vacuum with nothing to push against; on July 17, 1969, as Apollo 11 flew, it printed a correction.
On March 16, 1926, in Auburn, Massachusetts, Goddard's gasoline and liquid-oxygen rocket flew 2.5 seconds, rose 41 feet and landed 184 feet away.

title: How GPS finds you
description: GPS receivers only listen: they time one-way signals from at least four satellites, turn the delays into distances, and solve for position and time.

facts.text: GPS satellites broadcast one-way signals; receivers only listen and never transmit to them, and the civilian service is free to anyone worldwide.
At least 24 GPS satellites circle about 20,200 km up, each going around Earth twice a day, so at least four are in view from almost anywhere.
Each GPS satellite broadcasts its position and the time; a receiver turns each signal's travel time into distance, since the signals travel at the speed of light.
A precise GPS fix uses four satellites: three to find the position and one to correct the error in the receiver's clock; it gives latitude, longitude, altitude and time.

title: GPS clocks and relativity
description: GPS works only because its satellites carry very precise atomic clocks, corrected for relativity: a millionth of a second means about 300 meters.

facts.text: GPS satellites carry very precise atomic clocks, far more precise than the clock in a GPS receiver.
GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast: weaker gravity speeds them 45, orbital speed slows them 7; uncorrected, errors would grow about 10 km a day.
Light travels about 300 meters in a millionth of a second (the speed of light is 299,792,458 meters per second).

title: Traffic signals
description: Traffic lights take turns so conflicting movements never both get green, and wire loops in the road tell a signal when a car is waiting.

facts.text: In December 1868 a signal with semaphore arms and red and green gas lamps, worked by a constable, went up outside Parliament; in January 1869 it exploded.
The first electric traffic signal went up on August 5, 1914, at Euclid Avenue and East 105th Street in Cleveland: red and green lights, hand-switched from a booth.
The 1914 Cleveland signal was wired so that conflicting signals were impossible: crossing roads could not both get green.
Inductive loops, the most common signal sensor, are wire loops sawn into the road, energized by an electronics unit's oscillating circuit; a car's metal lowers the loop's inductance, calling a green.

title: Roundabouts
description: Roundabouts cut the points where drivers' paths cross from 32 to 8, remove right-angle and head-on crashes, and slow traffic, so far fewer crashes injure anyone.

facts.text: A four-way intersection has 32 vehicle conflict points; a single-lane roundabout has 8 and eliminates right-angle and left-turn head-on crashes.
Studies of US intersections converted to roundabouts found injury crashes fell by 72-80%.

title: How self-driving cars sense the road
description: Self-driving cars combine cameras, radar, lidar, GPS and detailed maps into a 3-D picture, and computers steer, brake and accelerate from it.

facts.text: On October 8, 2020, Waymo opened its fully driverless ride service, with no one at the wheel, to the public in the Phoenix area.
Autonomous vehicles use radar, GPS, cameras and lidar to build a 3-D map of their surroundings, and computers use it to adjust steering, speed and braking.
Self-driving cars also rely on highly detailed maps of the roads they drive.
Lidar (light detection and ranging) sends pulses of laser light and times their reflections to measure distance.

title: SAE levels of driving automation
description: SAE J3016 sorts driving automation into Levels 0 to 5, by who is driving: you at Levels 0-2, the system at Levels 3-5 when engaged.

facts.text: SAE J3016 defines six levels of driving automation, 0 to 5: at Levels 0-2 the human drives and must supervise; at Levels 3-5 the system drives when engaged.
At SAE Level 3 the car drives in limited conditions but the driver must take over when asked; Level 4 needs no takeover within its limits; Level 5 drives anywhere.
On June 8, 2023, California approved Mercedes-Benz Drive Pilot, a Level 3 system, for sale to the public: highways, daylight, up to 40 mph, driver takes over when prompted.
Britannica noted that, as of 2025, no car was fully autonomous.

title: The propeller
description: A propeller is a spinning wing: its blades make lift pointed forward, throwing air or water backward, so it needs a fluid to push and cannot work in space.

facts.text: A propeller acts like a rotating wing, making a lift force and accelerating air backward through it; its blades are twisted because the tips move faster than the hub.
Ship and aircraft propellers work the same way, rotating in water or air; the thrust depends on how much water or air they accelerate, and how fast.
Turbine engines and propellers push on air from the atmosphere, so they cannot work in space; rockets push on their own exhaust and can.

title: Gutenberg's printing system
description: Gutenberg combined reusable metal type, oil-based ink and a press into a system that printed pages again and again; movable type itself came first in China and Korea.

facts.text: Gutenberg's system combined durable, reusable metal type cast from an alloy that melts easily and cools quickly, a thick oil-based ink that clings to metal, and a press likely adapted from wine, oil or paper presses; set type could print a page again and again.
Movable type came before Gutenberg: in China, Bi Sheng (Pi Sheng) made it from baked clay in 1041-48, and Korea printed with metal movable type in the 14th century.

title: Printing spreads ideas
description: Cheap printed copies multiplied Europe's books into the millions by 1500 and let ideas such as Luther's theses spread in weeks.

facts.text: Before printing, Europe's manuscript (hand-copied) books numbered in the thousands; by 1500, after only 50 years of printing, there were more than 9 million books.
Luther dated his 95 theses October 31, 1517, for academic debate at Wittenberg; others translated and printed them, and thanks to printing they were known throughout Germany within a few weeks.

title: The electric telegraph
description: A telegraph key opens and closes a circuit, sending pulses of current that switch an electromagnet at the far end; Morse in the US and Cooke and Wheatstone in Britain built working systems.

facts.text: On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse sent "What hath God wrought!" by telegraph from the Capitol in Washington to his partner Alfred Vail in Baltimore.

In Morse's telegraph a key made and broke the circuit; at the receiver an electromagnet, switched on and off by the signals, moved a stylus that marked dots (short signals) and dashes (longer ones) on moving paper.
In 1837 Britain's William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented a telegraph with six wires and five needles; the current swung the needles to point at letters, using Oersted's discovery.

title: Morse code
description: Morse code spells letters with dots and dashes, giving the commonest letters the shortest codes; Morse and his partner Vail share the credit.

facts.text: Morse code spells letters with dots and dashes; E, the most frequent letter in English, got the shortest code: a single dot.
Britannica credits Morse with a dot-and-dash system in 1835, while his partner Alfred Vail made many contributions; the Franklin Institute credited Vail with the alphabet of dots and dashes itself.

title: How a telephone carries a voice
description: A telephone turns sound into a current that rises and falls like the sound wave, then turns it back into sound with an electromagnet and a diaphragm.

facts.text: On March 10, 1876, Bell's lab notes record the first intelligible speech by telephone: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."

A telephone's transmitter turns the vibrations of a diaphragm into a current that varies like the sound wave (an analogue signal); at the receiver the changing current in an electromagnet vibrates another diaphragm, recreating the sound.
Bell reasoned that a sound wave vibrating one membrane would induce a voltage in an electromagnetic coil, which would in turn make a second, connected membrane vibrate.

title: Who invented the telephone
description: Bell received the patent, but Gray filed on a similar idea the same day and Meucci had filed a caveat earlier, so the credit is still argued.

facts.text: Bell applied for his telephone patent on February 14, 1876; Britannica says Elisha Gray filed a caveat on a similar method hours later that day, though the order is disputed. Bell's patent was granted March 7, 1876.
Gray's caveat described a liquid transmitter, and Bell's first successful speech transmission, on March 10, 1876, also used a liquid transmitter.
In 2002 the US House of Representatives passed a resolution honoring Antonio Meucci's work on the telephone; it said he could not pay the $10 fee to keep his caveat after 1874.

title: How radio sends sound
description: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves made by changing currents in antennas; stations carry sound by varying a carrier wave (AM or FM).

facts.text: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, a form of light, with the longest wavelengths in the spectrum; they travel at the speed of light and need no medium, not even air.
A varying current in an antenna sends out electromagnetic waves at the speed of light; an incoming wave pushes electrons back and forth in a receiving antenna, making a small current.
Stations put sound on a radio-frequency carrier wave: AM varies the carrier's amplitude (strength) to match the sound, while FM keeps the amplitude constant and varies the frequency.
You tune a radio to a specific frequency, and the radio turns the waves it receives into vibrations of its speaker that make sound.

title: Who invented radio
description: Hertz made radio waves; Marconi, Popov and Tesla all have claims on radio, and even a 1943 US Supreme Court case weighed priority.

facts.text: On December 12, 1901, Marconi received the first radio signal sent across the Atlantic, from Cornwall to Newfoundland: the Morse letter S, three dots.
Heinrich Hertz first produced and transmitted radio waves; Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Ferdinand Braun.
On May 7, 1895, Aleksandr Popov demonstrated a radio receiver (a lightning detector) in St. Petersburg without knowing Marconi's work; Russia hails him as radio's inventor.
In 1943 the US Supreme Court held Marconi's key US tuning patent invalid as anticipated by earlier work, chiefly John Stone Stone's, and said Tesla had anticipated several of its features.

title: Scanning a picture
description: Television sends a picture as a signal by scanning it spot by spot and line by line, then rebuilding it in the same order fast enough to look whole.

facts.text: Early mechanical television pictures, like those of the 1920s, had only 30 lines, repeating about 12 times a second, and flickered badly.

Television sends a picture by scanning it spot by spot, left to right along a line and then one line lower, turning each spot's brightness into an electrical signal; the receiver rebuilds it in the same order, fast enough for the eye to see a whole picture.
In a cathode-ray picture tube, a beam of electrons sweeps the screen, and the picture signal applied to the electron guns controls how bright each spot glows.

title: Television's pioneers
description: Baird's mechanical system, Farnsworth's electronic camera tube and Zworykin's work at RCA all shaped television; no one person invented it.

facts.text: On January 26, 1926, John Logie Baird showed his mechanical "Televisor" to members of the Royal Institution in London: the first public demonstration of television.
Paul Nipkow's 1884 patent used a spinning disk punched with a spiral of holes, each hole scanning one line of the picture; mechanical systems like Baird's used such disks.
Philo Farnsworth concluded only an electronic system could scan fast enough, and made his first all-electronic TV transmission on September 7, 1927, with his image dissector camera tube.
Vladimir Zworykin filed for an all-electronic TV patent in 1923 and built the iconoscope camera tube at RCA after visiting Farnsworth's lab in 1930; in 1939 RCA agreed to pay Farnsworth royalties.
In February 1937 the BBC adopted the electronic Marconi-EMI system exclusively, dropping Baird's system.

title: How a camera forms an image
description: A camera is a dark box: light through a small opening or lens forms an image on a light-sensitive surface, as in the camera obscura.

facts.text: Camera obscura is Latin for 'dark chamber': the earliest were darkened rooms where light through a single tiny hole cast an upside-down image of the outside scene on the opposite wall.
A camera is a light-tight box with a lens that focuses light onto a light-sensitive surface (film, a plate or a sensor), plus an aperture and shutter that control how much light gets in.

title: Film and digital sensors
description: Film records light with silver salts that darken when developed; a digital sensor turns light at each pixel into an electric current that is measured and stored.

facts.text: Niepce's 1827 view from his window at Le Gras, made in a camera obscura on a bitumen-coated pewter plate, is the oldest surviving camera photograph; estimates of its exposure run from about eight hours to several days.
Film is coated with light-sensitive silver salts such as silver bromide; developing turns the light-struck crystals into dark metallic silver, so bright parts of a scene record dark: a negative.
Daguerre's process was announced on January 7, 1839; Britannica says that had Talbot announced his negative method a few weeks earlier, he would probably be known as photography's founder.
A digital camera has no film: when light strikes the pixels of its sensor (a CCD or CMOS chip), it induces an electric current that is measured and stored as digital data.
Willard Boyle and George Smith invented the CCD image sensor in 1969 and shared half of the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

title: Pixels and LCD screens
description: A screen image is a grid of pixels, millions on an HD or 4K screen; an LCD makes no light and uses liquid crystals to let a backlight through or block it.

facts.text: A pixel is the smallest unit of a screen image, with its own brightness and color; many tiny pixels seen from a normal distance blend into one continuous picture.
An HD screen is 1,920 x 1,080 pixels (about 2 million); a UHD '4K' screen is 3,840 x 2,160, four times as many (about 8.3 million).
An LCD makes no light of its own: a backlight shines through liquid crystals that change how much light passes when a voltage is applied, behind red, green and blue subpixel filters.

title: Mixing red, green and blue light
description: The eye has three kinds of cones, so screens can make a broad range of colors by mixing red, green and blue light.

facts.text: Color screens build each pixel from red, green and blue subpixels, and combinations of the three produce a broad range of hues.
Mixing light is additive: red and green light together look yellow, and red, green and blue together look white.
The eye has three types of cone cells, each most sensitive to a different range of wavelengths (roughly red, green and blue); the colors we see come from combinations of their signals.

title: Cells and base stations
description: A cellular network splits land into cells, each with a base station that talks to phones by radio; low-power signals let frequencies be reused.

facts.text: A cellular network divides its area into small cells, often drawn as hexagons; phones talk by radio waves to the base station serving their cell, and a switching office connects calls onward.
Because battery-powered phones transmit at low power, the frequencies used in one cell can be reused in other cells, multiplying the calls a network can carry.
The cellular concept was outlined in a 1947 Bell Laboratories technical memorandum.
On April 3, 1973, Motorola engineer Martin Cooper made the first handheld cell phone call, to Joel Engel of rival Bell Labs, on a 2.5-pound prototype.

title: Handoff between cells
description: As a phone moves from one cell to another during a call, the network automatically passes the call to the new cell.

facts.text: When a phone moves from one cell into another during a call, a central controller automatically reroutes the call to the new cell without a noticeable break: a handoff.

title: Inside a smartphone
description: A smartphone packs a phone, radio, camera and screen together with a speaker, a vibration motor and a rechargeable lithium-ion battery.

facts.text: A smartphone is a mobile phone with a display screen and an operating system that lets you install software (apps); most have a touchscreen and a built-in camera.
In a loudspeaker, a coil of wire in a strong magnetic field moves with the changing current and vibrates a diaphragm, which vibrates the air to make sound.
Phones buzz with tiny motors: an eccentric rotating mass motor spins an off-center weight, while a linear resonant actuator (used in iPhones) shakes a weight on a spring with a coil.
Lightweight, rechargeable lithium-ion batteries power mobile phones and laptops; Goodenough, Whittingham and Yoshino shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for them.

title: Capacitive touchscreens
description: A capacitive touchscreen senses where a conducting finger disturbs its electric field; insulators like plastic have no effect.

facts.text: On a capacitive touchscreen, your finger, which conducts electricity, alters an electric field by an amount that depends on where it is; these screens can sense several touches at once.
A plain plastic stylus does nothing on a capacitive screen, because plastic is an insulator and stops your hand from affecting the electric field.

title: Signals: electricity as a messenger
description: In communication technology, electricity carries information in the pattern of a current or wave: on-off pulses, or a continuous copy of a sound wave.

facts.text: A communication signal is a changing current, voltage or wave whose pattern stands for information: a telegraph's on-off pulses, or a telephone line's voltage that is an analogue of the sound wave.

title: What a computer is
description: A computer is a programmable machine for processing, storing and displaying information; the word once meant a person who calculated.

facts.text: Computer once meant a person who did computations; the word now almost always means automated electronic machinery.
From 1935, the NACA's Langley lab (NASA's forerunner) employed women as computers who read wind-tunnel data, ran calculations and plotted results; later they also programmed electronic computers.
Britannica defines a computer as a programmable device for processing, storing and displaying information; programmable means it follows a changeable set of instructions, a program.

title: Input, processing, memory, output
description: Every computer takes input, processes it in the CPU, holds data and instructions in memory, and sends out output.

facts.text: A computer has input devices such as a keyboard or mouse, a central processing unit (CPU) that processes data, memory that holds data and instructions, and output devices such as a screen or printer.

title: Counting in binary
description: Binary uses only 0 and 1 because a transistor switch is either on or off; each place is worth double the one before, and 8 bits make a byte.

facts.text: Computers use binary because the flow of electricity through a transistor switch has two states: on stands for 1 and off for 0.
In binary each place is worth double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128; for example 5 = 4 + 1 is written 101. Eight bits make a byte.
A byte's 8 bits can make 256 different patterns, from 00000000 to 11111111, standing for the numbers 0 to 255.

title: Letters and pictures as numbers
description: Computers store text, pictures and sound as binary: each letter gets a number (lowercase a is 01100001 in ASCII), and each pixel's color is stored as numbers.

facts.text: Computers store numbers, letters, colors, pictures and sounds in binary code, which uses only two symbols, 0 and 1; each 0 or 1 is called a bit.
ASCII is an 8-bit code: one byte stands for one letter, digit or punctuation mark, and lowercase a is 01100001.
A digital picture is a grid of tiny dots called pixels, and each dot's color is stored as numbers in binary.

title: Transistors and the microchip
description: A transistor is a tiny semiconductor switch flipped by a small electrical signal; an integrated circuit puts many of them, and their wiring, on one piece of silicon.

facts.text: A transistor is a semiconductor device; used as a switch, a small signal turns it on or off to control a larger current, and its on and off states stand for 1s and 0s.
John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley made the first working transistor at Bell Labs in December 1947.
Modern processors hold billions of transistors, microscopic electronic switches that turn on and off billions of times a second.

Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments (1958) and Robert Noyce at Fairchild (1959) independently invented the integrated circuit: many parts and their connections on one piece of semiconductor, usually silicon.

title: Moore's law
description: Moore's law is Gordon Moore's observation (1965, revised 1975) that chip transistor counts double about every two years; it is a trend the industry chased, not a law of nature.

facts.text: Intel's 4004 of 1971 was the first commercially available microprocessor: a whole CPU on one chip, with 2,300 transistors.
Apple's M1 chip, announced in November 2020, has 16 billion transistors.
From the 4004's 2,300 transistors (1971) to the M1's 16 billion (2020) is a rise of about 7 million times: almost 23 doublings in 49 years, about one every two years.
In 1965 Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, predicted the number of components on a chip would double every year; in 1975 he revised it to every two years.
Moore's law is an observation and forecast, not a law of nature: the chip industry adopted it as a target, making it partly a self-fulfilling prophecy.

title: Memory and storage
description: RAM is fast working memory that forgets without power; storage (hard drives and SSDs) keeps files for the long term with the power off.

facts.text: Main memory (RAM) holds the instructions and data of the programs that are running right now.
Most main memory (DRAM) is volatile: it loses its contents when the power is switched off.
Storage holds data and programs that are not in use, for the long term, and is nonvolatile: it keeps data with the power off.
A file you are editing sits in RAM; saving writes a copy to long-term storage, so unsaved work is lost if the power fails.
A hard drive stores bits on spinning platters, in tiny areas magnetized to store a 1 or demagnetized to store a 0; magnetism keeps the data with the power off.
A solid-state drive (SSD) stores data in nonvolatile flash memory chips and has no moving parts.

title: Software and code
description: Software is the instructions that tell hardware what to do; programmers write code in high-level languages that a compiler or interpreter translates into binary machine code.

facts.text: Software is the instructions that tell a computer what to do, its programs; the physical machine is called hardware.
A processor runs only machine code, instructions written in binary 0s and 1s that are hard for people to read and write; high-level languages such as Python and Java are much easier.
A compiler translates a whole program into machine code, saved to run whenever needed; an interpreter translates and runs it one instruction at a time.
Grace Hopper designed one of the first compilers after joining the Eckert-Mauchly Computer Corporation in 1949; in 1957 her team built Flow-Matic, the first English-language data-processing compiler.

title: Algorithms
description: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that solves a problem in a finite number of steps; a program is an algorithm written in code.

facts.text: The word algorithm comes from Algoritmi, the Latin form of the name of al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century mathematician, from the Latin translation of his arithmetic book.
An algorithm is a systematic procedure that solves a problem in a finite number of steps; long division is one.
In computer science, an algorithm is the sequence of steps a program follows; a map app's driving directions come from an algorithm.

title: Sorting algorithms
description: Different algorithms can solve the same problem with very different effort: selection sort work quadruples when the list doubles, merge sort work only slightly more than doubles.

facts.text: Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining item and moves it to the front; its work grows with the square of the list size, so doubling the list about quadruples it.
Merge sort splits a list in half, sorts each half the same way, then merges the sorted halves; its work grows as n log n, so doubling the list only slightly more than doubles it.

title: The first computers
description: There is no single first computer: Babbage's mechanical designs, the ABC, Zuse's Z3, Colossus and ENIAC were each first by a different measure.

facts.text: London's Science Museum built Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2, designed in 1847-1849, from his plans; the calculating section, finished in 1991, works as he intended.
Charles Babbage conceived the Analytical Engine in 1834: a mechanical machine to be programmed with punched cards, with a store for numbers and a mill for arithmetic. It was never built.
In 1843 Ada Lovelace published notes showing how the Analytical Engine could compute Bernoulli numbers, often called the first computer program; she saw it could handle letters and musical notes too.
The Atanasoff-Berry Computer, built at Iowa State in 1939-1942, was electronic but not programmable.
Konrad Zuse's Z3, completed in Germany in 1941, was the first working program-controlled computer; it was built from electromechanical relays, not electronics.
Colossus, working at Bletchley Park by February 1944 to break German codes, was the first digital, programmable, electronic computer, though only in a limited way; it stayed secret for decades.
ENIAC, completed by February 1946 in Philadelphia, was the first programmable general-purpose electronic digital computer.
In 1973 a US court ruled the ENIAC patent invalid, finding that its inventors had derived ideas from John Atanasoff's work.
Which machine was the first computer is disputed, because each early machine was first by a different measure: mechanical design, program control, electronics or general purpose.

title: From rooms to pockets
description: Transistors and then microprocessors shrank computers from 30-ton room-fillers to desktop personal computers to handheld smartphones.

facts.text: ENIAC, unveiled in February 1946, weighed about 30 tons, used about 18,000 vacuum tubes and filled a 50-by-30-foot room.
ENIAC lost a vacuum tube roughly every day or two, and with almost 18,000 tubes, finding the failed one was hard.
Transistors' small size, low heat, high reliability and low power use let them largely replace vacuum tubes by the late 1950s, making far smaller circuits possible.
Setting ENIAC up for each new problem meant connecting wires and setting switches by hand, which took days.
A personal computer is built for one person at a time; the market took off in 1977 with the mass-produced Apple II, TRS-80 and Commodore PET.
IBM's PC of 1981, with an Intel processor and Microsoft's MS-DOS operating system, became an industry standard.
A smartphone is essentially a handheld computer built into a mobile phone, with an operating system that runs installed apps.

title: Operating systems
description: An operating system manages a computer's resources, shares processor time among programs in tiny slices, and is loaded into memory at start-up.

facts.text: An operating system is the program that manages a computer's resources (processor, memory, file storage, input and output devices, network connections) and shares them among other programs.
Common operating systems include Windows, macOS and Linux on computers, and Android and iOS on phones.
A multitasking operating system gives each program a small time slice of processor time, about 20 milliseconds in Windows, then switches: about 50 slices a second, so programs seem to run at once.
When a computer is switched on, a start-up program stored on a chip, such as the BIOS, checks which devices are present and loads the operating system into main memory.

title: The instruction cycle and clock speed
description: A CPU runs one loop, fetch, decode, execute, from start-up to shutdown, paced by a clock that ticks billions of times a second.

facts.text: From start-up to shutdown, a CPU repeats the instruction cycle: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it means, execute it.
A CPU's control unit fetches instructions from memory in sequence, and its arithmetic-logic unit does arithmetic and logic operations such as comparing data.
Clock speed counts a CPU's cycles per second in gigahertz, billions per second: a 3.2 GHz CPU runs 3.2 billion cycles a second, though chip design matters too.
A 3.2 GHz processor clock ticks about 53 million times during each single cycle of 60-hertz grid power.

title: How the internet began
description: ARPANET, funded by the US Defense Department, sent its first message ("lo") in 1969 and grew into an internet now used by about 6 billion people.

facts.text: On October 29, 1969, UCLA tried to log in to the Stanford Research Institute over ARPANET; "lo" got through before the system crashed, and the full login worked about an hour later.
ARPANET was funded in the late 1960s by ARPA, an arm of the US Defense Department, and linked computers at universities and research sites.
By 1971 ARPANET had grown to 15 nodes.
On a 24-hour clock of the 3.3 million years of tools, ARPANET's 1969 message (57 years ago in 2026) lands about 1.5 seconds before midnight.
The ITU estimates that about 6 billion people, about three-quarters of the world's population, were using the internet in 2025.

title: TCP/IP: the network of networks
description: Cerf and Kahn's TCP (1974) let separate networks join into one; ARPANET switched to TCP/IP in 1983, and TCP resends lost packets.

facts.text: In 1974 Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn published TCP, a design for joining separately built packet networks (including radio and satellite ones) into one network of networks.
On January 1, 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, with every connected computer converting to the protocol at the same time.
TCP numbers the data it sends, so the receiver can put packets in order and spot gaps; lost packets are detected and sent again.

title: Packet switching
description: Data is chopped into small addressed packets that travel independently by any available route and are reassembled at the destination.

facts.text: Packet switching breaks a message into small packets that travel independently over any available route, across connected networks, and are reassembled at the destination.
Each packet carries the address of its destination.
A traditional phone call used circuit switching, holding one dedicated line for the whole conversation; packet switching needs no dedicated circuit, so lines are shared.

title: Where packets came from
description: Paul Baran (RAND) and Donald Davies (NPL) independently invented packet switching; Baran wanted a network that survived damage, and Davies named the packets.

facts.text: In the early 1960s Paul Baran at RAND worked on a US Air Force network that would not fail if one of its nodes was destroyed, routing messages along whichever path worked.
Donald Davies at Britain's National Physical Laboratory developed the same idea independently and named the pieces "packets" in a 1966 proposal.

title: Undersea internet cables
description: Over 99% of intercontinental data crosses the oceans in cables; anchors and fishing, not sharks, cause most faults, so traffic is spread across many cables.

facts.text: Undersea cables carry over 99% of the data that travels between continents, a figure TeleGeography confirmed in 2023.
Fishing vessels and ships dragging anchors cause about two-thirds of undersea cable faults.
Fish bites, sharks included, caused zero cable faults from 2007 to 2014, according to International Cable Protection Committee data.
Countries use multiple cables and networks spread traffic across several, so when one breaks, data keeps flowing over the others.
Satellites help reach places not yet wired, but cables carry far more data at a fraction of the cost; a phone is wireless only to the nearest cell tower, then fiber.
As of 2026, TeleGeography tracks more than 600 active and planned submarine cables.

title: Light in glass fibers
description: Undersea cables carry data as laser light in hair-thin glass fibers inside a cable about as wide as a garden hose.

facts.text: In modern undersea cables, lasers flash light down glass fibers about as thin as a human hair to receivers at the far end.
