The fibers are wrapped in plastic and sometimes steel wire; across the ocean a cable is typically about as wide as a garden hose.
In the deep sea, cables lie directly on the ocean floor; near shore they are buried under the seabed and given extra armor.

title: What Wi-Fi is
description: Wi-Fi carries data by radio over the short hop between your devices and the router; the modem links the home network to the provider.

facts.text: Wi-Fi is not short for "wireless fidelity": a marketing firm hired by the group now called the Wi-Fi Alliance coined it for its pleasing sound and echo of "hi-fi."
Wi-Fi uses radio waves to transfer data over short distances, usually less than 100 meters indoors.
A home router creates the local Wi-Fi network for your devices; the modem connects that network to your internet provider.
In 1997 the IEEE approved a common Wi-Fi standard, 802.11, so equipment from different makers could work together.

title: Wi-Fi bands
description: Routers use a 2.4 GHz band (longer reach, better through walls) and a 5 GHz band (faster, shorter range); 2.4 GHz is 2.4 billion cycles a second.

facts.text: Most routers offer a 2.4 GHz band, which reaches farther and passes walls better, and a 5 GHz band, which is faster but covers a shorter range.
A hertz is one cycle per second, so 2.4 GHz means 2.4 billion cycles a second: 40 million times US grid AC's 60.

title: The web versus the internet
description: The internet is the infrastructure; the web is one service that runs on it, like email.

facts.text: The internet is the infrastructure, a huge network of communicating computers; the web is one service built on top of it, and email is another.
ARPANET sent its first message in 1969 and the web was invented in 1989, 20 years later.

title: Inventing the World Wide Web
description: Tim Berners-Lee invented the web at CERN in 1989 using HTML, URLs and HTTP; CERN gave the software away in 1993.

facts.text: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 at CERN, to let scientists at universities and institutes around the world share information automatically.
By the end of 1990 Berners-Lee had the first web server and browser running; the server carried a handwritten label: "This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!"
Web pages are written in HTML, which includes hyperlinks to related information; each page has an address called a URL; HTTP standardizes how servers and browsers talk.
On April 30, 1993, CERN put the World Wide Web software in the public domain, which helped the web flourish.

title: Crawling and indexing
description: Search engines send crawlers along links and build an index, like a book's, that searches look through instead of the live web.

facts.text: When you search, Google looks through webpages already organized in its Search index, not the live web.
Search engines use software called crawlers that automatically visit public web pages and follow the links on them, organizing what they find into an index.
Google's index works like the index at the back of a book, with an entry for every word on every indexed page; it covers hundreds of billions of pages.

title: Ranking search results
description: BackRub, which became Google, treated links as votes; ranking today weighs many signals such as meaning, relevance, quality and location.

facts.text: As Stanford graduate students, Sergey Brin and Larry Page built BackRub, which counted links as votes; a link from a heavily linked site was a stronger vote. It grew into Google.
Google's ranking today weighs many signals, including the meaning of your query, relevance and quality of pages, usability, and context such as your location.

title: What the cloud is
description: The cloud is on-demand access over the network to shared computers and storage in data centers.

facts.text: NIST defines cloud computing as on-demand network access to a shared pool of computing resources (servers, storage, applications) that can be quickly provisioned and released.
Cloud services run on computers and storage systems housed in data centers, buildings reached over the internet.

title: Data centers and energy
description: Data centers used about 415 TWh (around 1.5% of world electricity) in 2024; most of it ends up as heat, and cooling can take up to 40%.

facts.text: The IEA estimates data centers used about 415 terawatt-hours in 2024, which is 415 billion kilowatt-hours and around 1.5% of the world's electricity.
Per unit of floor space, data centers use 10 to 50 times the energy of a typical office building, says the US Department of Energy.
Most of the electricity a data center uses ends up as heat, and cooling can account for up to 40% of its energy.

title: Encryption basics
description: Encryption uses an algorithm and a key to turn plaintext into ciphertext; Caesar's shift cipher is a simple, easily broken example.

facts.text: Encryption uses an algorithm and a key to turn readable plaintext into ciphertext, so only the intended recipient, holding the right key, can read it.
Julius Caesar replaced each letter with the one three places down the alphabet; with only 25 possible shifts, the cipher is easy to break.

title: Public-key encryption
description: Diffie and Hellman (1976) showed how to keep messages secret with no prearranged key; public-key cryptography uses one key to lock and another to unlock.

facts.text: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman's 1976 paper gave a blueprint for communicating over an open channel, with no prearrangement, while keeping messages secret from eavesdroppers.
Public-key cryptography uses two separate keys: one to encrypt the data and a different one to decrypt it.
The "https" and padlock icon in a browser's address bar indicate that traffic to the site is encrypted.
Public-key cryptography became the backbone of modern internet security; it lets your browser check that your bank is really who it claims to be.

title: How accounts get attacked
description: Most account break-ins rely on phishing, reused leaked passwords (credential stuffing) and guessing predictable passwords.

facts.text: NIST notes that rules demanding capitals, digits and symbols push people toward predictable passwords like "Password1!", which attackers are likely to guess.
Phishing messages try to get you to open harmful links or hand over personal information; warning signs include urgent language and look-alike addresses such as amazan.com.
In credential stuffing, username and password pairs leaked in one breach are tried on other websites.
Attackers try common passwords and ones from previous breaches first.
Phishing sites increasingly use HTTPS certificates too, so the FBI warns not to trust a site just because it shows a padlock.

title: Protecting your accounts
description: Current NIST and CISA guidance: long passwords or passphrases, a different one for every account, a password manager, and multifactor authentication.

facts.text: NIST's 2025 guidance (SP 800-63B-4) treats length as a primary factor in password strength and requires at least 15 characters when a password is used alone.
Under NIST's 2025 rules, sites should not force mixes of character types or require password changes on a schedule, only when there is evidence of compromise.
CISA recommends passwords of at least 16 characters, such as a passphrase of 4 to 7 unrelated words, and a different password for every account.
A password manager generates, stores and fills in your passwords, and NIST notes managers make people likelier to choose stronger passwords.
Multifactor authentication requires two or more ways to prove it is you; CISA rates security keys best against phishing, and text or email codes weakest.

title: How long the internet takes
description: Light in optical fiber covers about a kilometer every 5 millionths of a second, so 1,000 km takes about 5 thousandths of a second.

facts.text: Light crosses a kilometer of vacuum in about 3.34 millionths of a second but takes about 4.9 (roughly 5) millionths in optical fiber, about two-thirds as fast.
At about 5 millionths of a second per kilometer, 1,000 km of fiber takes about 5 thousandths of a second and 10,000 km about a twentieth of a second, one way.

title: A fridge moves heat
description: A refrigerator does not make cold: it forces heat out of its cold inside and releases it into the room, which is why an open fridge door warms a kitchen.

facts.text: A refrigerator takes heat from its cold inside and releases it into the room, so the area behind a running fridge feels warmer than the room.
Heat does not flow on its own from a cold place to a warmer one; a fridge forces it to by doing work on a refrigerant.
With the fridge door open, heat just circles from the room through the fridge and back out, while the running motor adds heat, so the room gets warmer.

title: The refrigerant loop
description: A fridge's refrigerant evaporates inside, soaking up heat, then is compressed so it condenses in outside coils and gives that heat up; the loop repeats.

facts.text: When a liquid evaporates, it draws energy from its surroundings, which cool down.
A fridge's refrigerant evaporates in pipes inside, absorbing heat; a compressor then squeezes the vapor so it condenses in coils outside the cold box and releases the heat, and the loop repeats.

title: How a microwave oven heats food
description: A magnetron fills a metal box with microwaves whose field tugs food's water molecules back and forth about 2.45 billion times a second; their jostling is heat.

facts.text: In 1945, Raytheon engineer Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar in his pocket melting near a running magnetron, a radar tube, and then used it to pop corn.
In 1947 Raytheon built the first microwave oven, the Radarange.
A magnetron inside a microwave oven makes microwaves at about 2,450 megahertz, a field that flips about 2.45 billion times a second.
Water molecules have a slightly negative oxygen end and a slightly positive hydrogen end; the microwaves' changing field twists them back and forth, and their jostling makes heat.
Microwaves are reflected by metal, pass through glass, paper and plastic, and are absorbed by food.
US safety rules require microwave ovens to have two independent interlocks that stop the microwaves the moment the door is opened.

title: Microwaves are non-ionizing
description: Microwaves, like visible light and radio waves, are non-ionizing: too weak to knock electrons out of atoms. Their energy becomes heat and doesn't make food radioactive.

facts.text: Microwaves, like visible light and radio waves, are non-ionizing radiation: they lack the energy to knock electrons out of atoms, unlike X-rays.
Microwave energy turns into heat as food absorbs it and does not make food radioactive.

title: How tap water is treated
description: Treatment plants clump dirt with coagulation and flocculation, let the clumps settle, filter the water through sand, gravel or charcoal, and then disinfect it.

facts.text: Coagulation adds chemicals that make dirt and small particles bind together; gentle mixing (flocculation) grows heavier clumps called flocs, which settle out (sedimentation).
Filters of sand, gravel or charcoal with different pore sizes then remove remaining particles and germs such as parasites, bacteria and viruses.

title: Germs in water, and killing them
description: Snow showed in 1854 that cholera spread through contaminated water; today plants disinfect with chlorine or chloramine, a practice US cities began in 1908.

facts.text: In 1854 John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London's Soho and found them clustered around a water pump on Broad Street; the pump's handle was then removed.
When Snow did his work, most doctors thought disease spread through bad air, called miasma, and didn't yet understand germs; Snow showed cholera spread through water contaminated with sewage.
Water plants add disinfectants such as chlorine or chloramine to kill remaining germs, including germs living in the pipes between the plant and your tap.
In 1908 Jersey City, New Jersey, became the first US city to routinely disinfect its community drinking water, and thousands of towns followed within a decade.
US typhoid fever fell from about 100 cases per 100,000 people in 1900 to 33.8 per 100,000 in 1920 as water treatment spread.

title: London's sewers and the Great Stink
description: The Great Stink of 1858 pushed Parliament to fund Bazalgette's sewers, built to remove 'bad air'; the 1866 cholera outbreak hit only unconnected areas, proving Snow right.

facts.text: In the hot summer of 1858, the stench of sewage in the River Thames, the 'Great Stink', overwhelmed people nearby and disrupted Parliament's business.
The Great Stink led Parliament to fund a new London-wide sewer system, overseen by the engineer Joseph Bazalgette, which London still relies on.
London's authorities built the sewers believing sewage caused disease-spreading bad air, before they accepted Snow's water theory.
London's last cholera outbreak, in 1866, struck parts of east London that were not yet connected to Bazalgette's sewers, the final proof of Snow's theory.

title: How a sewage plant cleans wastewater
description: Gravity carries sewage to a plant; screens and settling tanks remove solids, microbes eat the organic material, and the water is disinfected and released.

facts.text: Sewers mostly use gravity to carry wastewater to treatment plants, which are built on low ground, often beside a river.
Treatment plants first screen out large debris, then let sludge settle to the bottom of tanks and skim floating grease and oil off the top.
In secondary treatment, air is bubbled into tanks so microorganisms naturally present in sewage can thrive and eat much of the organic material.
Treated wastewater is disinfected with chlorine or bleach and then released into a river or the ocean.

title: Air conditioning
description: Air conditioners work like a fridge for a whole house, moving heat from indoors to outdoors; Carrier's 1902 system was built to control humidity at a printer.

facts.text: In 1902 engineer Willis Carrier designed a system with cooling coils to fix a humidity problem spoiling printed pages at a Brooklyn printing company, the first modern electrical air conditioning.
Air conditioners and heat pumps work on the same principle as a refrigerator: refrigerant moves heat from a cooler place to a warmer one.

title: Heat pumps
description: A heat pump moves heat either way: out of the house in summer and in from the cool outdoors in winter, delivering about 3 kWh of heat per 1 kWh of electricity.

facts.text: In summer a heat pump moves heat from your home to the outdoors; in winter it collects heat from the cool outdoors and concentrates it inside.
An electric resistance heater turns 1 kWh of electricity into 1 kWh of heat, but 1 kWh used in a heat pump can move about 3 kWh of heat into a house.
Because heat pumps transfer heat rather than generate it, they are much more efficient than traditional heating systems.

title: How vaccines train the immune system
description: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form, piece or blueprint of a germ; it makes antibodies and remembers, so a later infection is stopped fast.

facts.text: A vaccine contains a killed or weakened germ, a piece of one, or genetic instructions (RNA or DNA) for making a piece; the immune system recognizes it, makes antibodies and remembers it, without the illness.
Antibodies are proteins the immune system makes to fight disease.

If a vaccinated person later meets the real germ, the immune system can destroy it quickly before they become unwell; protection can last years, decades or a lifetime, preventing disease rather than treating it.

title: Vaccines: history and safety record
description: Jenner's 1796 smallpox vaccine led to smallpox's eradication in 1980; vaccines pass clinical trials before use and are monitored after, and WHO calls them very safe.

facts.text: In 1796 Edward Jenner created the first successful vaccine, against smallpox, after noticing that milkmaids who had caught cowpox did not catch smallpox.
After a worldwide campaign of vaccination and tracking cases, WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980, the only human infectious disease ever eradicated.
Before use, each vaccine goes through several phases of clinical trials involving thousands of volunteers, and once in use its safety is monitored continuously.
WHO describes vaccines as very safe: side effects are usually minor and brief, such as a sore arm or mild fever, and serious ones are extremely rare.
WHO reports that over the past 50 years, vaccines against 14 diseases have saved at least 154 million lives.

title: X-rays and CT scans
description: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by calcium-rich bone, which shows white; CT spins an X-ray beam around the body to build slices and 3D images.

facts.text: Wilhelm Rontgen discovered X-rays in 1895, and on 22 December 1895 he made an X-ray image of his wife's hand showing her bones and a ring.
Doctors quickly took up X-rays to look inside the body without surgery.
X-rays carry more energy than visible light and pass through most of the body, but calcium-rich bones absorb more of them, so bones appear white while fat, muscle and lungs show as shades of gray.
X-rays are ionizing radiation, which can harm living tissue, though the cancer risk from an X-ray exposure is generally considered very small.
A CT scanner rotates a narrow X-ray beam around the body, and a computer turns the signals into cross-sectional slices that can be stacked into a 3D image.

title: MRI scans
description: MRI lines up protons in the body's water with a powerful magnet, knocks them with radio pulses and reads the energy they release; no ionizing radiation.

facts.text: An MRI scanner's powerful magnet lines up protons in the body's water; radio pulses knock them out of line, and sensors detect the energy they release as they realign.
MRI uses no ionizing radiation and shows soft tissues such as the brain, nerves and ligaments more clearly than X-rays or CT.
An MRI scanner's magnetic field is strong enough to fling a wheelchair across the room.

title: How antibiotics kill bacteria
description: Antibiotics hit structures bacteria have and human cells lack; penicillin, found by Fleming in 1928, stops bacteria building cell walls so they burst. They don't work on viruses.

facts.text: In 1928 Alexander Fleming saw that bacteria would not grow where a culture had been accidentally contaminated by Penicillium mold; the mold made penicillin.
Penicillin stops bacteria from building their cell walls, leaving them leaky and fragile so they burst; human cells have no such walls.
Antibiotics do not work on viruses, such as those that cause colds and flu, because viruses lack the bacterial structures antibiotics attack.

title: Antibiotic resistance
description: Resistance means the bacteria, not your body, learn to beat a drug: resistant survivors multiply. WHO: about 1 in 6 lab-confirmed bacterial infections resisted antibiotics in 2023.

facts.text: Antibiotic resistance happens when germs such as bacteria develop the ability to defeat the drugs designed to kill them; it doesn't mean your body becomes resistant.
When antibiotics are used, resistant germs survive, multiply and can pass resistance traits in their DNA to other germs.
In his 1945 Nobel lecture, Fleming warned that exposing microbes to penicillin doses too small to kill them could make them resistant.
WHO reports that about 1 in 6 lab-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide were resistant to antibiotics in 2023.
CDC's 2019 report estimated more than 2.8 million antimicrobial-resistant infections and more than 35,000 deaths in the US each year.
WHO names the misuse and overuse of antibiotics as one of the main drivers of resistance.

title: What plastic is
description: Plastics are polymers, long chains of repeating units, mostly built from fossil-fuel carbon; Baekeland's 1907 Bakelite was the first fully synthetic plastic.

facts.text: In the 1860s a billiards company offered a $10,000 prize for a substitute for ivory billiard balls; John Wesley Hyatt took it up, and his work led to celluloid, one of the first plastics.
Polymer means 'of many parts': a plastic is made of long chains of repeating units, and the length of those chains makes it strong, light and flexible.
Most synthetic polymers are made from carbon supplied by petroleum and other fossil fuels.
Leo Baekeland invented Bakelite in 1907, the first fully synthetic plastic, made of no molecules found in nature.

title: Why plastic lasts
description: Microbes' enzymes don't recognize plastic's bonds, so plastic doesn't rot: it breaks into smaller pieces, down to microplastics under five millimeters.

facts.text: Microbes break down natural polymers such as lignin in plants using enzymes, but those enzymes don't recognize the bonds that hold plastic polymers together.
Outdoors, plastic breaks into smaller and smaller pieces but doesn't fully biodegrade for thousands of years.
Plastic pieces less than five millimeters long, about the size of a pencil eraser, are called microplastics, and most plastic in the ocean breaks up into such small particles.

title: Germ theory
description: Germ theory says microorganisms that invade and multiply in the body cause infectious disease; Pasteur and Koch established it, and it underpins disinfection, vaccines and antibiotics.

facts.text: Germ theory is the principle that infectious diseases are caused by microorganisms, such as bacteria and viruses, that invade the body and multiply.
In the mid-1800s Louis Pasteur showed that microbes cause fermentation and rotting; in 1882 Robert Koch showed a bacterium causes tuberculosis, and he soon identified the cholera germ too.
Germ theory laid the foundation for disinfection, antiseptics, vaccines and antibiotics.

title: The skyscraper frame
description: A steel skeleton, not the walls, carries a tall building's weight, so walls stop thickening with height and hang on as curtain walls.

facts.text: In a load-bearing building the walls carry the floors above; the earliest skyscrapers rested on extremely thick masonry walls at ground level, which ate usable floor space.

The north half of Chicago's Monadnock Building (finished 1891) is 16 stories of load-bearing brick, with walls about 2 meters (6 feet) thick at the base; it is generally regarded as the tallest office building held up by its walls.

Chicago's 10-story Home Insurance Building (1884-85), designed by William Le Baron Jenney, is generally considered the first tall building held up by an internal iron and steel skeleton of columns and beams.
In a frame building the outer wall is a curtain wall: it bears only its own weight and hangs on the skeleton, so it no longer has to thicken as the building rises.

title: The tallest building record
description: Height records change, so they carry a date: as of 2026 CTBUH ranks Burj Khalifa (2010, 828 m) the tallest.

facts.text: As of 2026, the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH) ranks Dubai's Burj Khalifa, completed in 2010, as the world's tallest building at 828 meters.
CTBUH measures a building's height to its architectural top, which counts spires but not antennas.

title: The safety elevator
description: Otis's brake gripped the guide rails when the rope lost its pull; the safe passenger elevator made tall buildings practical.

facts.text: In 1854 at the Crystal Palace in New York, Elisha Otis rode his elevator platform high above the crowd and ordered the rope cut; his safety device stopped the fall.
Otis's safety device clamped onto the guide rails the car ran on when tension was released from the hoist rope, so a broken rope itself set the brake.
In modern elevators a speed governor trips the safety if the car moves down too fast, and brakes clamp onto the guide rails.
The first safe passenger elevator, installed in 1857 in the E.V. Haughwout store in New York City, made buildings of more than four or five stories practical.

title: The elevator counterweight
description: A counterweight about equal to the car half full hangs on the other end of the cables, so the motor lifts only the difference.

facts.text: In a traction elevator a motor turns a grooved wheel, the sheave, that moves the cables holding the car and the counterweight; as the car goes up, the counterweight goes down.
An elevator's counterweight weighs roughly as much as the car loaded half full, so the motor lifts only the difference in weight, plus a little extra to overcome friction.

title: Tension and compression
description: Structures resist two basic forces: tension pulls and stretches, compression pushes and squeezes; a bending beam has both.

facts.text: Structures such as bridges must resist two basic forces: tension, which pulls and stretches, and compression, which pushes and squeezes.
When a beam bridge bends under a load, its top is squeezed in compression and its bottom is stretched in tension.

title: Arch and suspension bridges
description: An arch carries loads by compression into massive supports; a suspension bridge hangs its deck from cables in tension; the longest span is dated and changes.

facts.text: An arch bridge carries loads mainly by compression, pressing down and outward (thrust) into supports massive enough to take it.
In a suspension bridge the deck hangs from curved cables in tension; the cables pass the load to towers, which carry it to the ground in compression, and to anchorages at the ends.
As of 2026, the world's longest suspension bridge span is 2,023 meters: Turkey's 1915 Canakkale Bridge, opened in 2022.
The 1915 Canakkale Bridge took the longest-span record from Japan's Akashi Kaikyo Bridge (1998); China's Zhangjinggao Yangtze River Bridge, with a planned 2,300-meter span, is due around 2028.

title: Concrete and reinforced concrete
description: Concrete is sand and gravel bound by cement that hardens by reacting with water; weak in tension, it gets steel bars inside.

facts.text: Cement sets and hardens by hydration, a chemical combination of its compounds with water, not by drying; construction cements will even set and harden under water.
Concrete is aggregate, usually sand and gravel, bonded together by cement and water; all else equal, less water makes stronger concrete.
Concrete is the second most-used substance in the world, after water.

Plain concrete handles compression but not tension, which makes it unsuitable for most structures on its own; reinforced concrete embeds steel, whose tensile strength works with concrete's compressive strength.

title: Roman concrete
description: The Pantheon's dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome; a 2023 MIT-led study found lime clasts that can help Roman concrete heal cracks.

facts.text: Rome's Pantheon, built around 128 CE and almost 1,900 years old, still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.

A 2023 MIT-led study of Roman concrete from Privernum found that its white lime clasts formed by hot mixing with quicklime; when cracks reach them and water gets in, dissolved calcium refills the crack as calcium carbonate.
In the 2023 study, deliberately cracked concrete made by hot mixing healed its cracks within two weeks, while matching concrete made without quicklime did not.

title: Brunel's tunnelling shield
description: Inspired by shipworms, Brunel's shield let miners dig small patches while the tunnel behind was lined; it built the first tunnel under a navigable river.

facts.text: Around 1812 Marc Brunel saw ship's timber riddled with tunnels bored by shipworms and took them as the inspiration for a protected way of tunnelling.
Versions of Brunel's tunnelling shield have been used in almost every major tunnel built since.
Brunel patented the tunnelling shield in 1818: miners in separate cells dug the face a patch at a time, then the shield moved forward while masons lined the new tunnel with brick behind it.
The Thames Tunnel in London, begun in 1825 and opened in 1843, was the world's first tunnel under a navigable river.

title: Tunnel boring machines
description: A TBM cuts the face with a rotating cutterhead and lines the tunnel with concrete rings as it goes; tunnel records are dated.

facts.text: A tunnel boring machine cuts the face with a rotating cutterhead and, behind it, installs precast concrete segments in rings to line the tunnel as it advances.
HS2's Euston tunnel boring machine is 198 meters long and works around the clock as an underground factory; HS2's machines average about 16 meters a day.
As of 2026, Switzerland's 57 km Gotthard Base Tunnel, opened in 2016, is the world's longest railway tunnel; tunnel boring machines dug most of it.
The Channel Tunnel between Britain and France, opened in 1994, is 50 km long, with about 38 km (37.8 km) under the sea, the longest undersea stretch of any tunnel.

title: Iron, carbon and steel
description: Steel is iron with up to about 2 percent carbon; cast iron, with 2 to 4 percent, is brittle and weak in tension.

facts.text: Steel is iron alloyed with carbon, up to about 2 percent; pure iron is soft, and carbon makes it much harder.
Cast iron has 2 to 4 percent carbon; it bears loads well in compression but is brittle and weak in tension.
Steel is by far the most widely used material for building the world's infrastructure and industries.

title: The Bessemer process
description: From 1856, blowing air through molten iron burned out extra carbon in minutes, using the reaction's own heat, and made steel cheap.

facts.text: In 1856 Henry Bessemer patented a process that made steel from molten iron in minutes and far more cheaply than before, turning steel from a costly material into one for mass use.
In the Bessemer process air is blown through molten pig iron, and its oxygen burns out extra carbon and other impurities; the heat of those reactions keeps the metal molten with no added fuel.
Cheap Bessemer steel revolutionized building construction and replaced iron in railroad rails and many other uses.
While the Home Insurance Building was going up, rolled-steel beams were substituted for some of its iron.

title: The moving assembly line
description: Ford's 1913 line brought the car to workers who each did a small repeated task, cutting Model T assembly from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes.

facts.text: In 1913 at Ford's Highland Park plant, the moving assembly line pulled each car along, at first by a rope and later by a moving chain, past workers who built it step by step.
Ford's engineers adapted the "disassembly line" that slaughterhouses used to take carcasses apart step by step, running the idea in reverse to build cars.
Ford combined interchangeable parts with work split into small repeated tasks and a steady flow of materials to create the moving assembly line; each worker did one or two tasks.
The moving assembly line cut the time to build a Model T from more than 12 hours to about 90 minutes.

title: Mass production and its costs
description: Making Model Ts in huge numbers cut the price from $850 to as little as $260, but the repetitive line drove workers away until the $5 day.

facts.text: Mass production let Ford cut the Model T's price from $850 to as little as $260; the company built over 15 million Model Ts from 1908 to 1927.
Doing one or two tasks over and over drove workers to quit, so in 1914 Ford announced $5 for an eight-hour day, up from $2.34 for a nine-hour day.

title: The industrial robot
description: Unimate, the first factory robot, went to work at General Motors in 1961 handling hot die-cast parts; about 5 million robots worked in factories in 2025.

facts.text: The word robot comes from Karel Capek's 1920 play R.U.R.; the Czech robota means forced labor.
Unimate, the first industrial robot, started work in 1961 at a General Motors plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey, lifting hot metal parts from a die-casting machine and stacking them.
Unimate followed step-by-step commands stored on a magnetic drum and could repeat a sequence of motions again and again; George Devol invented it and Joseph Engelberger helped build the company.
The International Federation of Robotics counted about 5 million industrial robots operating in factories worldwide in 2025.

title: Teaching a factory robot
description: A programmer teaches a robot its task with a teach pendant and it repeats it precisely; robots took dangerous, repetitive jobs and are fenced off from workers.

facts.text: A trained programmer typically uses a handheld teach pendant to teach an industrial robot its task, guiding it through the moves; the robot then repeats them with high accuracy.
Industrial robots take the place of workers in dangerous or repetitive tasks such as moving materials, welding, painting and loading machine tools.
Workers are kept out of an industrial robot's restricted space by safeguards such as fixed barriers, interlocked gates and presence-sensing devices.

title: Additive manufacturing
description: 3D printing builds an object layer upon layer from a digital model instead of cutting material away, which suits prototypes and one-person custom parts.

facts.text: Additive manufacturing (3D printing) builds objects layer upon layer from a digital 3D model, unlike subtractive methods such as drilling, cutting and milling that remove material.
3D printers are widely used to make complex components in a wide variety of materials.
3D printing is a leading technology for rapid prototyping and is used for custom, patient-specific items such as hearing aids, dental aligners, implants and prosthetics.

title: How 3D printing began
description: Hull's 1983 stereolithography hardened liquid polymer with UV light layer by layer (SLA-1, 1987); Crump's glue-gun frog led to FDM in 1989.

facts.text: In 1988 Scott Crump tried to make a toy frog for his young daughter with a glue gun loaded with polyethylene and candle wax, building the shape layer by layer.
In 1983 Chuck Hull developed stereolithography, which hardens liquid photopolymer with ultraviolet light one layer at a time.
Hull's stereolithography patent was issued in 1986, the year he co-founded 3D Systems, which introduced the SLA-1, the first 3D printer made for commercial sale, in 1987.
Crump patented fused deposition modeling in 1989; it squeezes melted plastic through a moving head, building a model from the bottom up, and Stratasys produced the first FDM machine in 1991.

title: The climbing tower crane
description: A tower crane grows with its building by jacking up its top and lifting in a new mast section; counterweights on its short arm balance the load.

facts.text: A tower crane grows one mast section at a time: a climbing frame jacks the top of the crane up about 6 meters (20 feet), and the crane lifts a new mast section into the gap to be bolted in.
A tower crane's short machinery arm carries large concrete counterweights that balance the loads its long working arm lifts.

title: What AI is
description: Artificial intelligence is a computer doing tasks we associate with intelligent beings; early wins like Deep Blue's 1997 chess victory came from brute-force speed.

facts.text: Britannica defines artificial intelligence as the ability of a digital computer or computer-controlled robot to perform tasks commonly associated with intelligent beings.
John McCarthy coined the term "artificial intelligence" in 1955.
In May 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov 3.5 to 2.5, winning by brute-force computing power: it could evaluate 200 million chess positions per second.

title: Machine learning
description: Machine learning trains a model on examples instead of hand-written rules; the model learns what its data teaches, including its gaps and biases.

facts.text: Machine learning trains software called a model to make predictions from data: shown examples labeled with the right answers, such as emails marked spam or not spam, it learns the patterns linking inputs to answers and applies them to new cases.
NIST warned in 2022 that biases embedded in the data used to train AI become embedded in the AI, and that algorithms trained on one type of data often cannot extrapolate beyond it.

title: How language models write
description: A large language model splits text into tokens and writes by predicting a likely next token, adding it and repeating; it learned this from huge amounts of text.

facts.text: Britannica describes large language models as advanced versions of predictive text: they aim to produce the most probable words for a given prompt.
Language models process text as tokens, basic units usually a few characters long, and write a reply by predicting a likely next token, adding it and repeating.
Large language models are trained on huge amounts of text, trillions of tokens, and the first ones followed the introduction of the transformer design in 2017.
On November 30, 2022, OpenAI introduced ChatGPT, a model fine-tuned with reinforcement learning from human feedback to interact in a conversational way.

title: Confidently wrong
description: Because a language model predicts likely-sounding text rather than checking facts, it can state false things confidently: a hallucination.

facts.text: Large language models sometimes present false or misleading information as fact, which is called a hallucination.
On June 22, 2023, a US federal judge in New York fined two lawyers and their firm $5,000 after they filed a brief citing six court cases that did not exist; ChatGPT had fabricated them.

title: How a VR headset works
description: A VR headset shows each eye a slightly different image for depth and uses motion sensors to redraw the view as your head moves; mismatched signals can cause motion sickness.

facts.text: In the late 1960s, Harvard's Ivan Sutherland built a head-mounted display jokingly called the Sword of Damocles because of the large overhead beam needed to support its weight; users explored a 3D wire-frame room by moving their heads.

VR headsets show each eye its own, slightly offset image, and the brain fuses the two into one picture with depth, as it does with the two views from our eyes; lenses let the eyes focus on screens so close.
VR systems use motion sensors to track the user's movements and adjust the view accordingly, usually in real time.
Motion sickness comes from conflicting signals: the eyes report motion while the inner ear senses stillness; some people get it from video games and virtual reality.

title: Augmented reality
description: Augmented reality adds computer-made images to your view of the real world instead of replacing it, from TV's first-down line to Pokemon GO.

facts.text: Augmented reality overlays computer-generated images on the real scene, viewed through devices such as smartphones, tablets, smart glasses and headsets; virtual reality instead creates an artificial environment.
Among the earliest mainstream uses of augmented reality was the yellow first-down marker added to American football broadcasts in the mid-1990s.
Pokemon GO, launched in 2016, used GPS data and the phone's camera to place Pokemon in real-world locations: augmented reality.

title: How a quadcopter flies
description: A quadcopter's four propellers push air down for lift; two spin each way so their twisting forces cancel, and it steers only by changing propeller speeds under a flight computer's control.

facts.text: A quadcopter's four spinning propellers push air downward, and by Newton's third law the air pushes the quadcopter up.

A spinning rotor twists an aircraft's body the opposite way (torque), so helicopters need a tail rotor; a quadcopter instead spins two propellers clockwise and two counterclockwise so the twists cancel.

A quadcopter steers with its propellers alone: speeding up the propellers on one side lifts that side, so it tilts and moves toward the side with less lift; speeding up one spinning pair over the other makes it rotate.

A drone's flight controller is an onboard computer that reads sensors such as gyroscopes and accelerometers, compares the drone's position, heading and orientation with its programmed plan, and applies control inputs to hold its course.

title: What drones are used for
description: Drones carry out jobs such as delivering blood to hospitals in Rwanda (from 2016) and counting birds and watching volcanoes for the USGS.

facts.text: On October 14, 2016, Rwanda launched the world's first national drone delivery service, flying blood to 21 transfusing facilities with drones built and operated by the US company Zipline.
The US Geological Survey uses drones for missions such as estimating migratory bird populations and monitoring volcanoes.

title: How CRISPR edits genes
description: CRISPR-Cas9, borrowed from a bacterial defense against viruses, uses a guide RNA to lead the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA sequence and cut it; the cell's repair machinery then makes the edit.

facts.text: CRISPR-Cas9 comes from a bacterial immune defense: bacteria store pieces of viral DNA in CRISPR arrays, make RNA that recognizes the virus if it returns, and use the enzyme Cas9 to cut the virus's DNA.

In CRISPR gene editing, a short guide RNA matches a target DNA sequence and leads Cas9 there to cut the DNA; researchers then use the cell's own repair machinery to delete, add or change genetic material.
Jennifer Doudna, Emmanuelle Charpentier and colleagues showed CRISPR could be used for gene editing in 2012; Doudna and Charpentier shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

title: Casgevy, the first CRISPR medicine
description: Casgevy, approved in the UK in November 2023 and the US in December 2023, edits a sickle cell patient's own blood stem cells to make fetal hemoglobin.

facts.text: In November 2023, the UK's medicines regulator (MHRA) authorized Casgevy, the world's first approval of a CRISPR-based therapy.

On December 8, 2023, the US FDA approved Casgevy for sickle cell disease in patients 12 and older: the patient's own blood stem cells are edited with CRISPR/Cas9 to make more fetal hemoglobin, then returned after high-dose chemotherapy.

title: The gene-editing line
description: Editing body cells affects one patient; editing eggs, sperm or embryos could pass changes to future generations, which the 2023 genome editing summit called unacceptable at this time.

facts.text: Most genome editing changes somatic (body) cells; changes to egg or sperm cells or to an embryo could be passed to future generations, and such editing is illegal in the United States and many other countries.
In 2018, He Jiankui announced twin girls born from gene-edited embryos in China; in December 2019 a Chinese court sentenced him to three years in prison.

In March 2023, the organizers of the Third International Summit on Human Genome Editing, including the Royal Society and the US National Academies, stated: "Heritable human genome editing remains unacceptable at this time."

title: Fusion versus fission
description: Fusion joins very light nuclei, such as the hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium, into helium; fission splits heavy nuclei such as uranium.

facts.text: Nuclear fusion joins light nuclei, such as hydrogen, into heavier ones, releasing a lot of energy; it powers the Sun and other stars. Fission, by contrast, splits heavy nuclei such as uranium.
The most efficient fusion reaction in the lab joins two hydrogen isotopes, deuterium and tritium, producing helium.
Unlike fission, fusion cannot undergo a runaway chain reaction or meltdown: if control of the plasma is lost, the reaction stops.

title: Why fusion is hard
description: Positively charged nuclei repel, so fusion fuel must be heated to about 150 million degrees C, becoming a plasma that has to be held by magnetic fields or squeezed by lasers.

facts.text: For fusion, nuclei must have enough energy to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between their positive charges, which requires heating the fuel to extreme temperatures, where it becomes a plasma.
ITER says deuterium-tritium fusion in the laboratory needs temperatures of 150,000,000 °C, 10 times hotter than the core of the Sun.
Fusion experiments contain the hot plasma either with magnetic fields, as in a tokamak, or by inertial confinement, squeezing fuel with lasers as the National Ignition Facility does.

title: NIF's 2022 ignition
description: On December 5, 2022, NIF's lasers delivered 2.05 MJ to a fusion target and got 3.15 MJ back: gain on the target, while the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid.

facts.text: On December 5, 2022, 192 laser beams at the National Ignition Facility (Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, California) delivered 2.05 MJ of energy to a fusion target, and fusion released 3.15 MJ: more energy out than the laser energy in, a gain above 1.5.
NIF's lasers need about 300 MJ of electricity from the grid to make each shot of about 2 MJ, so the December 2022 result was a gain on the target, not net energy for the facility.
NIF's 3.15 MJ fusion yield is under one kilowatt-hour (3.15 / 3.6 = about 0.875 kWh), since a kilowatt-hour is 3.6 million joules.

title: Qubits
description: A qubit can be 0, 1 or a mix of both (superposition), but measuring it always gives a plain 0 or 1.

facts.text: A classical bit is either 0 or 1, but a qubit can be in state 0, state 1 or a mix of the two (a superposition); when measured, it gives either 0 or 1.

title: What quantum computers are (and aren't) for
description: Quantum computers are expected to help with specific jobs such as simulating molecules and factoring huge numbers, not to replace ordinary computers; qubits are fragile and error-prone.

facts.text: In 2019, Google researchers reported that their Sycamore quantum processor did a calculation in 200 seconds that they estimated would take a top supercomputer 10,000 years; IBM researchers argued a better classical method could do it in 2.5 days.

NIST expects quantum computers to be useful for specific problems, such as simulating the quantum rules that govern molecules, chemicals and materials, and says quantum and classical machines could work together rather than one replacing the other.
In 1994, Peter Shor described a quantum algorithm that could quickly factor the huge numbers that protect much of today's encryption.
In August 2024, NIST released its first finalized encryption standards designed to withstand attacks by quantum computers.
Qubits are fragile: many must be kept at temperatures near absolute zero, and quantum computers make an error roughly once in every thousand operations, far more often than classical computers.
The 2019 test task was sampling the output of random quantum circuits, a benchmark chosen because it grows exponentially harder for classical computers.

title: Space spinoffs
description: NASA research gave everyday life technologies such as the CMOS image sensor in phone cameras and memory foam, recorded in NASA's yearly Spinoff report since 1976.

facts.text: In the 1990s, Eric Fossum's team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory developed CMOS active pixel image sensors, a camera on a chip that was smaller and used far less power than older sensors; cell phones became their killer application.
NASA has published Spinoff, profiling space technologies that benefit life on Earth, every year since 1976.

Memory foam began in 1966, when Charles Yost, working with NASA's Ames Research Center, developed a "slow spring back" foam for airplane seats that gave better crash protection; it later padded football helmets, helped prevent bedsores and cushioned shoe insoles.

title: Spinoff myths
description: Tang, Teflon and Velcro are not NASA inventions; astronauts used them, which made people link them with space.

facts.text: NASA did not invent Tang, Teflon or Velcro: General Foods developed Tang in 1957, DuPont invented Teflon in 1938, and a Swiss engineer invented Velcro in the 1940s.
The myths grew from use in space: John Glenn drank Tang in orbit in 1962, and Apollo missions used Velcro extensively to anchor equipment.

title: Weighing a new technology
description: Every technology trades benefits against costs; asking who benefits, who bears the risk and who supplies the evidence helps judge it, as leaded petrol and the War of the Currents show.

facts.text: From 1922, tetraethyllead was added to petrol to improve engine performance; it harmed health, including heart disease, stroke and children's brain development, and its use ended worldwide when Algeria stopped selling it in July 2021, 99 years later.

Most high-income countries had banned leaded petrol by the 1980s, but as late as 2002 almost all low- and middle-income countries still used it; UNEP estimates ending it prevents more than 1.2 million premature deaths a year.

title: The Collingridge dilemma
description: David Collingridge's 1980 dilemma: early on, a technology is easy to change but its effects are hard to foresee; once the effects are clear, it is entrenched and hard to change.

facts.text: In his 1980 book The Social Control of Technology, David Collingridge described a dilemma: a technology's effects are hard to predict until it is widely used, but by then it is entrenched and hard to change.

title: Rules matched to risk
description: The EU's AI Act, in force since August 2024, bans a few AI uses, strictly regulates high-risk ones like hiring and leaves most everyday AI, such as spam filters, free of new obligations.

facts.text: The European Union's AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024; it bans a few AI practices such as social scoring, sets strict obligations for high-risk uses such as hiring, and places no obligations on minimal-risk AI such as spam filters.
